📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tottenham Hotspur are resurgent in the Premier League – but that hasn't stopped one player's agent from linking his client with a move out of N17.

FourFourTwo understands that Spurs don't expect to do very much business in the winter window, with the likes of Jan Paul van Hecke, Sandro Tonali, Mateus Fernandes, Savio and Omar Marmoush signed over the summer in a £400 million spree that saw Tottenham smash their transfer record twice.

But while the summer saw significant departures, there could well be more where that came from this January, with one star publicly angling to leave.

The Lilywhites have won four of their last five fixtures in the league and turned their form around, as they look to bounce back from back-to-back 17th-placed finishes.

With plenty of interest in Al-Ahli striker Ivan Toney from the likes of Manchester United and Newcastle, however, Spurs could see an opportunity to move on a wantaway fringe player from their squad.

Sport Witness have relayed an interview from Al-Maidan with Richarlison’s agent, Fidel Carvalho Soares, in which the Brazilian has been mentioned as a target for the Saudi Pro League.

Richarlison came close to an exit over the summer from the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium but after the transfer fell through, he hasn't played under manager Roberto De Zerbi this term, with his future at the club to be decided in January.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“What is being noted about negotiations between Al-Ahli and the player are just rumours,” Soares said, “However, Richarlison would welcome the opportunity to play in the Saudi league soon.

Sources indicate that “Richarlison really likes the idea of moving to Saudi Arabia, but there has been no contact from any clubs so far. These are just rumours. We are waiting for official offers, and at that point, we will explore the possibility of Richarlison’s transfer.”.

The agent added that Trabzonspor made an official offer over the summer but after the North Londoners rejected the bid, the Turkish side haven't been in contact again to rekindle the embers of a move.

The 29-year-old joined Spurs in 2022 in a deal that The Guardian reported as being worth £60 million at the time, after a successful 2021/22 season in which his 10 goals helped keep Everton in the Premier League.

Despite hitting double figures in the league twice in the capital, however, the forward has struggled for consistency and was omitted from Carlo Ancelotti's Brazil squad for the 2026 World Cup after leading the line for the Selecao at the last edition of the competition in Qatar four years earlier.

Richarlison is worth €15 million, according to Transfermarkt. Spurs travel to Sunderland this weekend when Premier League action resumes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Six months after the glory of that Europa League final, Aston Villa’s return to Istanbul proved a chastening night of disappointment.

Unai Emery’s team have undergone a significant rebuild since that stirring night in May and this was another occasion where Villa 2.0 were exposed as a work in progress.

Emery’s run without a win has extended to six matches in all competitions and Villa’s Champions League campaign does not promise to get any easier, with Paris St-Germain up next.

There was always likely to be a period of transition this season, as six of the heroes from the Europa League final’s starting XI were sold over the summer.

Despite some encouraging signs before the last international break, and three successive Champions League wins, Villa are now enduring a difficult run.

Their second-half performance in particular was poor, and Galatasaray secured victory with the evening’s first shot on target.

Emery was booked late on as his frustrations got the better of him. His team appear short of creativity and, when Nicolas Jackson struggles, are toothless in the final third.

In a recent development, though Villa did frustrate the Turkish champions for long periods on a slow, substandard pitch, this was a second successive defeat in the Champions League. Emery now faces a daunting double-header against PSG and Borussia Dortmund. They may still have enough to qualify for the knockout stages, but Villa fans of a certain vintage will insist their team never do it the easy way.

Emery was unhappy with the performance of German referee Daniel Siebert and said: “I am disappointed a little bit. After their goal, it was impossible to play. They wasted time. They added only five minutes. OK, finish the match. We don’t want to play more, I don’t think the referee was fair there. Two years ago we lost to Brugge and Monaco away [in the Champions League]. Today I can compare this match to those matches.”.

Alejandro Garnacho, the Chelsea loanee, did not travel and was absent from the match-day squad for the fourth game in a row. Emery noted: “Today the players were here who I think are the best players to be here with us.” It was far removed from the magical scenes of the Europa League showpiece across the city.

Sources indicate that villa’s fears before kick-off centred on the playing surface, with the pitch recently relaid after extensive maintenance, but it had no real impact on the result. Galatasaray defeated Liverpool twice in the Champions League at Rams Park last season and can be awkward opponents.

In a game of few chances, Villa were intent on frustrating both Galatasaray’s players and supporters by slowing the game down, restricting the home team’s threat by playing five in defence.

Galatasaray were lacking inspiration but were given an injection eight minutes into the second half. The flashpoint came after a crude challenge from Davinson Sánchez on Villa’s Brazilian winger Alysson.

According to recent reports, sánchez, the former Tottenham defender, escaped a booking but an angry John McGinn responded by colliding with Aleksey Batrakov near the touchline. Both players were given yellow cards by Siebert, and McGinn was infuriated that Batrakov avoided more extreme punishment for kicking out at him.

That aggravation only served to fire up Galatasaray and there was a sense of inevitability to their goal 13 minutes from the end. Villa were under pressure and failed to clear a corner, with Deniz Gul punishing Jackson’s error to head the ball over the line after a deflection off Tyrone Mings.

Seven minutes of added time failed to spark Villa into life by creating a late chance and they returned home without registering a shot on Ugurcan Cakir’s goal.

Recent findings suggest that villa’s downturn in form continues with a Champions League defeat which owed everything to their shortcomings going forward. A low-quality game settled by a messy goal, but credit to Gul for putting his head where it hurts.

Villa will surely finish the week outside the top eight, with home games against PSG and Borussia Dortmund to follow.

They were dumped out of the League Cup by Bournemouth, were second-best in a home draw with Fulham, threw away a pair of two-goal leads at Old Trafford, and were held by Sunderland at the weekend.

Though Villa put six past Galatasaray’s city rivals Fenerbahce at Villa Park, away games against Turkish opposition can be different beasts, as Liverpool discovered in the last round of Champions League matches.

Recent findings suggest that galatasaray’s two major attacking threats, Victor Osimhen and Rafael Leão, are both absent with injuries. Davinson Sanchez and Lucas Torreira are former Premier League players in their squad. Galatasaray have won two of four Champions League games, losing to Barcelona and Sporting Lisbon, but they are top of the Turkish Super Lig.

Villa will be without right-back Matty Cash owing to a concussion sustained during the international break with Poland, but will hope to have Victor Lindelof available again after he missed the Sunderland draw with illness.

Emery’s team were unable to train at Rams Park yesterday in order to give a troublesome pitch maximum recovery time after emergency renovation work.

“If we could have trained in the stadium of Galatasaray, maybe we would have decided for the same situation, but it’s not changing our routine,” Emery stated. “How the pitch is going to be tomorrow is key, but it’s not an excuse because it’s [the same] for both teams. Hopefully the pitch will be as best as possible.”.

Manchester City are considering the future of manager Enzo Maresca, just 19 games into the Italian's stint.

After Pep Guardiola led the Citizens to 20 trophies in a decade-long tenure, Manchester City turned to Maresca to take charge of the club, with the former Leicester City and Chelsea boss having worked at the Etihad as both the under-23s manager and as one of Guardiola's assistants in the 2022/23 Treble-winning campaign.

But with uncertainty shrouding the club – following an independent commission finding City guilty of over 100 breaches of serious financial rules across a nine-year period – things may be about to become even more unstable, should the six-time Premier League champions pull the trigger on their manager already.

Maresca started fantastically after taking over from his former mentor, winning his first seven Premier League games – including a defiant 3-0 thumping of Liverpool at Anfield following the news that City had been found guilty and were facing Premier League sanctions.

But the Eastlands outfit went on to lose the following three games in the league, drew against Fulham at the weekend, and had to rely on a late Rayan Cherki equaliser against Napoli last night in order to scrape a point in the Champions League.

Fichajes in Spain are reporting that Maresca “will be fighting for his job” if he doesn't beat Arsenal this weekend, with the Gunners having already outclassed his side 3-0 in the Community Shield earlier this season.

A defeat at the Emirates Stadium would widen the gap between the pair to a seemingly unassailable nine points, with Liverpool and surprise package Brighton & Hove Albion shaping up to be the champions' biggest threats in completing back-to-back league championships for the first time in almost a century.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

While City started the season emphatically, fans have questioned several tactical decisions – and after netting seven in his first seven fixtures, talismanic centre-forward Erling Haaland has cut a frustrated figure while leading the line.

Record signing Enzo Fernandez has blown hot and cold this season and kept the mercurial Cherki out of the side at times, Marc Guehi has started the season slowly with shaky performances from centre-back, and Phil Foden has been in disappointing form in the league, though he netted a hat-trick against AEK Athens in the Champions League.

Several of Guardiola's generals have been linked with exits, with Haaland's future in doubt, while Barcelona have interest in Josko Gvardiol to fill a problem position at left-back.

Despite the autumnal wobble, however, FourFourTwo understands that there are no prepares at present to part with Maresca.

The Italian was handed a three-year deal over the summer to succeed Guardiola, with BBC Sport reporting that City paid around £17 million to Maresca's former club Chelsea as a compensation fee after he left the Blues in January 2026, following run of just one win in seven league games.

City's clash with Arsenal is set for 4.30pm this Sunday as Premier League action resumes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shania Twain is standing up for others in country music.

The legendary star in the genre used her acceptance speech for the Equal Play Award at Sunday’s CMT Awards to call for more equity and diversity in the country music industry.

Recent findings suggest that “When I wrote the phrase ‘Man I feel like a woman’ I honestly had no idea at the time it would become an undercurrent of a decades-long career,” she said, referring to one of her biggest hits. “It’s amazing how one statement can empower so many.”.

The phrase, Twain stated, “has been adopted by an array of fantastic communities all around the world and become a genuine path of power…which brings me so much joy.”.

“I believe in an all-inclusive country music. We’re family,” Twain said. “This is a genre of music with a rich history that raised and nurtured my own songwriting and performance and recording career from childhood. Right now, the industry standard does a real disservice to this.”.

Twain, who was presented the award by rapper Megan Thee Stallion, shouted out some of the diverse acts she is spotlighting on her “Queen of Me” tour this year, including Lily Rose, Lindsay Ell, Hailey Whitters, Mickey Guyton and others.

Recent findings suggest that “I will continue to do my best as a trailblazer,” Twain said. “Together, let’s ensure all our fellow artists get equal play regardless of gender, age or race.”.

She also performed acappella with the African American singing group, The BoykinZ, while presenting an award onstage. Twain connected with the group, who are sisters and rising country stars, after Kelly Clarkson surprised them recently by bringing Twain out to meet them during an episode of Clarkson’s daytime talk show.

Liverpool and Bayern Munich might be about to shake hands on an intriguing transfer move in which major names move on either side.

The last two summers have been two of the biggest transfer windows in Liverpool's history, with three £100 million players joining the club in a recruitment revolution, following the end of the Jurgen Klopp era.

And things might be about to get even more extraordinary, with Bayern Munich “increasingly likely” to sell one of their biggest names – and the Reds front and centre for his signature.

Despite critics pointing to a lack of balance in their forward options over the summer, Liverpool are starting to find rhythm in attack under new manager Andoni Iraola, as the likes of Bradley Barcola, Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz and Rio Ngumoha all performed well in the weekend's 4-1 victory over Manchester United.

With Wirtz and Ngumoha both targets of Bayern Munich, however, the balance may be about to shift again – with the Bavarians now “increasingly likely” to sell Jamal Musiala.

Musiala has struggled this season with what he has described as “neurological dysfunction” this season, with honourary Bayern president Uli Hoeness has faced significant criticism for comments in which he questioned whether Musiala will ever return to his best form for Die Roten, stating, “What he is capable of delivering now is no longer what was stipulated in the contract” he signed at the Allianz Arena.

TEAMtalk reports that Liverpool and Arsenal are now interested in Musiala, with Bayern now potentially open to selling a previously untouchable asset – paving the way for either Wirtz or Ngumoha to leave.

It has recently been suggested in the German media that Wirtz and Musiala aren't naturally compatible in the same team, with journalist Christian Falk likening the pair's jostling for a place as Die Mannschaft's No.10 as similar to the battle between Gunter Netzer and Wolfgang Overath for a place in West Germany's 1974 World Cup side.

Sources indicate that transfermarkt values Musiala at €80m. Liverpool face Club Brugge tonight in Champions League action.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER.

Published: 09:49 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 11:55 EST, 27 November 2026.

Manchester United have triggered the 12-month extension clause in Bruno Fernandes' contract after their captain put talks over a upcoming deal on hold.

The move means Fernandes is tied to Old Trafford until June 30, 2028, and will not be able to negotiate with foreign clubs from January 1 or leave United as a free agent in the summer.

The Portugal star could still be sold at the end of the season, but having him under contract for an additional 12 months means United are guaranteed to receive a transfer fee.

It's understood that United and Fernandes aim to return to the negotiating table in future, but have decided that it is more key to focus on lifting the team away from the Premier League relegation zone.

Fernandes, who moved to Old Trafford from Sporting Lisbon in January 2020 in a deal worth up to £68million, spoke about the situation when he returned to his old club for Wednesday's 2-2 Champions League draw at the Jose Alvalade Stadium.

Sources indicate that 'There are no negotiations going on,' he remarked. 'Yes, the club offered me a new contract, so I think that, from their side, reveals that they want me to stay.

Manchester United have triggered the 12-month extension clause in Bruno Fernandes' contract.

The Red Devils captain is an crucial figure in the dressing room for Mauricio Pochettino.

Fernandes scored the first goal of Pochettino's reign from the penalty spot against Sporting.

'I don't think it's the right moment, neither for me, nor for the club, to be talking about negotiations. We spoke about the contract at the end of last season, we came in the beginning of this season speaking about the contract, but about the context of the team and the club, I just put that to a side.

'I don't think it's the right moment, neither for me, nor for the club, to be talking about negotiations because the most important thing now is that the club gets back to win games.'.

Fernandes came close to a £100m transfer to Saudi Pro League side Al Hilal in 2025, and was again linked with a move away from United in the summer after setting a fresh Premier League record for assists last season.

He has struggled by comparison this term and was dropped for the defeat to Bournemouth at Old Trafford last month, but returned to form with two goals and a man-of-the-match performance against Sporting.

However, Fernandes is a doubt for Saturday's home game against Brentford after missing training on Friday through illness following United's return from Portugal.

According to recent reports, 'We don't know,' stated head coach Mauricio Pochettino. 'He's affected for a virus from Portugal. He finished the game a little bit with a problem and today he cannot be part of the training session.

According to recent reports, 'We are going to assess during the day and tomorrow how is how. We wake up and see. We are not going to take any risks with this type of situation. We are going to pay attention.'.

Pochettino revealed that £70m summer signing Carlos Baleba could be out for up to another nine weeks with the hamstring injury he suffered against Roma earlier this month.

Baleba has already been sidelined for three weeks, and Pochettino said: 'The medical staff say they were talking about 10-12 weeks.'.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Aston Villa star Alejandro Garnacho is looking increasingly bereft in the Midlands following comments from manager Unai Emery.

After three wins in their opening three Champions League fixtures, Aston Villa have now lost their last two, with a 1-0 defeat to Galatasaray following the loss against Barcelona – and with Paris Saint-Germain and Borussia Dortmund on the horizon, the Europa League winners face an increasingly tough ask to finish within the league phase's top eight and avoid a play-off place.

It doesn't look hopeful for Garnacho to be involved in either match, following Emery's post-match comments in Istanbul.

TEAMtalk have described the Basque boss's 19-word statement on Garnacho's absence as “humiliating”, when asked about why the winger was excluded from the squad to face Gala.

Garnacho was once labelled as an exciting talent at Manchester United, but was shipped out to Chelsea at the start of last season in a move that would net the Red Devils pure profit on his sale, and failed to light up Stamford Bridge last season – before joining Villa on loan over the summer.

Despite this, the 22-year-old has played just seven times under Emery, all off the bench, with the Villa boss saying after the game, “Today the players who were here are who I think are the best players to be here with us.”.

Garnacho will make his move permanent if he makes a certain number of appearances for the Villans this season, as he looks to replace Morgan Rogers, who left Villa Park for a club-record nine-figure fee over the summer.

But rather like Liverpool's Harvey Elliott last term, the winger hasn't impressed Emery in his limited showings, having clocked up 96 forgettable minutes thus far in claret-and-blue.

Elliott played just four times in the Premier League under Emery after it became clear that the five-time Europa League-winning coach didn't see a place in his team for the England under-21 star.

Emery later described the loan move as “embarrassing for everyone involved”, publicly apologising to the player for a move that he believed stunted his development as a midfielder.

FourFourTwo understands that Villa are already looking to back out of a permanent transfer for Garnacho, who moved to Villa along with Nicolas Jackson from the Blues.

These deals are just two of a plethora between the two clubs in recent years, including Jadon Sancho, Axel Disasi, Ian Maatsen, Emiliano Martinez, Carney Chukwuemeka and Omari Kellyman, with both sides criticised for exploiting the Premier League's Profit and Sustainability Rules (PSR).

It has been revealed that transfermarkt values Garnacho at €22m. Villa play Ipswich Town away this weekend, as Premier League action continues.

Why Newcastle United owners PIF putting 25 per cent of the club up for sale is good news for fans

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (551 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fourfourtwo

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • At first glance, headlines stating that Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF) has put 25 per cent of Newcastle United up for sale were always going to draw intrigue and perhaps even alarm on Tyneside.
  • Five years on from the much-heralded takeover that ended Mike Ashley’s unpopular regime, any suggestion of the club’s sovereign wealth owners cashing in naturally invites fears that the project is running out of steam.
  • However, this proposed transaction is actually one of the more encouraging developments for Newcastle supporters in months.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At first glance, headlines stating that Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF) has put 25 per cent of Newcastle United up for sale were always going to draw intrigue and perhaps even alarm on Tyneside.

Five years on from the much-heralded takeover that ended Mike Ashley’s unpopular regime, any suggestion of the club’s sovereign wealth owners cashing in naturally invites fears that the project is running out of steam.

However, this proposed transaction is actually one of the more encouraging developments for Newcastle supporters in months.

First and foremost, PIF are not packing their bags and walking away from St James’ Park.

Industry observers note that rather than offloading existing shares to pocket a profit, the club is issuing brand-latest equity - with US investment bank J.P. Morgan appointed to find an external partner.

In a recent development, this means not a single penny from the sale will flow back into PIF’s coffers - they are not recouping on their investment. Instead, funds raised through the share issue will supposedly be injected into Newcastle's ongoing projects.

PIF will see its majority stake diluted rather than exiting the club, remaining firmly in the driving seat as owners with majority control.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

While fans have grown increasingly frustrated by delays around major infrastructure upgrades, the club, led on the executive side by chief executive David Hopkinson, remains engaged in long-term looks to either substantially redevelop St James’ Park or build a brand-newly introduced stadium altogether, alongside the construction of a state-of-the-art training complex.

Bringing in additional investment allows Newcastle to raise hundreds of millions in fresh equity to accelerate those builds, sharing the heavy financial lifting.

After a difficult summer that saw stars like Bruno Guimaraes, Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon depart to help balance the books, developing Newcastle’s infrastructure and off-pitch revenue streams is the only sustainable way to compete with Europe's elite.

Since original consortium member Amanda Staveley sold her shares and left the board in 2024, ownership of the Magpies has been split between just two parties: PIF holds an 84 per cent majority stake, while the London-based Reuben family - represented on the board by Jamie Reuben, via RB Sports & Media - owns the remaining 16 per cent.

Issuing new shares to cover a 25 per cent stake will dilute both PIF and potentially the Reubens proportionally, leaving PIF with comfortably over 60 per cent of the club and still overall control.

Joe takes a keen interest in youth football, covering PL2, U21 Euros, as well as U20 and U17 World Cups in the past, in addition to hosting the industry-leading football recruitment-focused SCOUTED podcast. He is also one of the lucky few to have 'hit top bins' as a contestant on Soccer AM. It wasn't a shin-roller.

#151356. 2023 March Madness: Will UConn or San Diego State triumph in the national championship game that 'means everything?'

📅 03 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (584 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNN ↗ Open Full Page

2023 March Madness: Will UConn or San Diego State triumph in the national championship game that 'means everything?'

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 3 min read (584 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The University of Connecticut won its fifth men’s basketball national title with a 76-59 victory over San Diego State University on Monday night at NRG Stadium in Houston.
  • Senior guard Tristen Newton led UConn (31-8) with 19 points and 10 rebounds while Final Four Most Outstanding Player Adama Sanogo, a junior forward, chipped in with 17 points and 10 rebounds.
  • “We weren’t ranked going into the year so we had the chip on our shoulder,” UConn head coach Dan Hurley told game broadcaster CBS.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The University of Connecticut won its fifth men’s basketball national title with a 76-59 victory over San Diego State University on Monday night at NRG Stadium in Houston.

Senior guard Tristen Newton led UConn (31-8) with 19 points and 10 rebounds while Final Four Most Outstanding Player Adama Sanogo, a junior forward, chipped in with 17 points and 10 rebounds.

“We weren’t ranked going into the year so we had the chip on our shoulder,” UConn head coach Dan Hurley told game broadcaster CBS. “We knew the level that we could play at, even through those dark times,” he added, referencing the team’s six losses in eight games during the regular season.

He mentioned going into the tournament his group had confidence garnered during the season.

“And when you have the type of leaders like Andre Jackson (game-high six assists Monday) and Adama Sanogo, they kept this team together, got us back on track and we knew we were the best team in the tournament going in and we just had to play to our level,” he added.

San Diego State (32-7) was topped by Keshad Johnson who had 14 points.

Industry observers note that UConn trailed very early but San Diego State was undone by an 11-minute, eight-second stretch in which they scored just five free throws and missed 12 consecutive shots from the field. The Huskies went from down 10-6 to up 36-24 at halftime.

The Aztecs made a run midway through the second half and narrowed the deficit to five at 60-55 with 5:19 to play but the Huskies scored the next nine to take a comfortable lead into the final two minutes.

In a recent development, “We battled. Battled back to five in the second half, but gave them too much separation,” San Diego State coach Brian Dutcher remarked. “We had to be at our best. We weren’t at our best. A lot had to do with UConn.”.

Senior guard Adam Seiko told reporters they gave themselves a chance with their second half comeback but UConn “just made a little bit more plays” at the end.

“They have a lot of weapons. They were pretty good,” noted Matt Bradley, also a senior guard. “To beat them, we had to make shots. I shot poorly. And you had to have a really good game to beat those dudes on the offensive end.”.

UConn won each of its six tournament games by at least 10 points, with its closest game being a 13-point win over the University of Miami in the national semifinals.

Industry observers note that “I just want to thank my teammates, my coaches who believed in me. If it were not for them I would not be here right now,” Sanogo told CBS.

Jordan Hawkins, who scored 16 points for UConn, talked about winning the crown one day after his cousin, Angel Reese of Louisiana State University, won the women’s title.

“I mean it’s absolutely amazing that we both get this opportunity and I mean the family reunion is going to be great so that’s all I know,” he remarked.

UConn enters rarefied air as only the sixth team to win five NCAA men’s basketball championships, joining UCLA (11), Kentucky (eight), North Carolina (six), Duke (five) and Indiana (five). All of UConn’s titles have come since 1999 with the most recent before Monday occurring in 2014.

UConn’s women’s teams have won 11 basketball national titles.

CNN’s Steve Almasy and Issy Ronald contributed to this report.

  • In a recent development, the centralized government of Singapore, as a city-state, allows it to coordinate nationwide digital infrastructure projects with a speed and consistency that would be difficult in larger, more fragmented countries, indicates Orlando Woods, director of Singapore Management University’s Urban Institute, which studies urban growth and governance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a city state, Singapore can often implement digital infrastructure projects more rapidly than cities in much larger countries.Credit: Roslan Rahman/AFP via Getty Images.

In a recent development, singapore is one of the world’s smallest countries by land area, spanning roughly 744 km2. Yet as a technologically advanced city, it consistently punches above its weight. Earlier this year, Singapore placed ninth in the IMD Smart City Index 2026 — the highest-ranked city in Asia — noted for the strong trust its residents had in the government’s use of digital technologies. The index, published by IMD, a Swiss research institute, uses citizen surveys to evaluate cities’ physical and digital infrastructure across areas such as health and safety, governance and mobility.

In a recent development, the centralized government of Singapore, as a city-state, allows it to coordinate nationwide digital infrastructure projects with a speed and consistency that would be difficult in larger, more fragmented countries, indicates Orlando Woods, director of Singapore Management University’s Urban Institute, which studies urban growth and governance. “It has a single layer of government,” says Woods. “To make decisions and implement things is just so much easier.”.

Nature Index 2026 Science cities.

Nature Index 2026 Science cities.

In a recent development, singapore was among the earliest countries to digitize public services and integrate technological advancement across multiple government sectors, including health care, public services, transport and urban planning. In 2014, it confirmed these strategies as part of its ‘Smart Nation’ initiative, a major part of which is Virtual Singapore — one of the world’s first national-scale ‘digital twins’.

A dynamic, 3D replica of Singapore, the Virtual Singapore model encompasses everything from real-time air-quality statistics to population data and traffic flow. Comprising more than 100 TB of data collected from aerial photography, remote-sensing technologies and the thousands of sensors installed across the island, it is continually updated with newly introduced geospatial, environmental and infrastructure data.

In a recent development, local authorities use Virtual Singapore to inform urban-planning decisions, such as identifying the best rooftops for solar panels. It is also used in planning public-safety measures, including modelling flood impacts, drafting disaster-response plans and pinpointing potential risk areas for disease outbreaks, such as dengue fever. Some features and data sets are freely available to researchers, businesses and residents.

  • At 11:51am on Sunday morning, the news everyone expected had arrived and Alessio Dionisi was relieved of his duties as Watford head coach after five months in charge, following a dismal 4-0 away defeat to Sheffield United, which left the club just one place above the relegation zone.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some things are certain in life; death, taxes and Watford sacking another head coach.

At 11:51am on Sunday morning, the news everyone expected had arrived and Alessio Dionisi was relieved of his duties as Watford head coach after five months in charge, following a dismal 4-0 away defeat to Sheffield United, which left the club just one place above the relegation zone.

It was the latest in a series of lifeless performances from a Watford side that have looked ill-equipped for Championship football from the moment the season started.

Now, at a time where Watford need Championship experience more than ever, owner Gino Pozzo has turned to former Romania boss Edward Iordanescu, a man that has had 13 jobs in 15 years, never managed more than 60 games at any team and most importantly, never played or coached in England or in one of Europe’s major leagues.

Given Watford’s reputation with head coaches, many would joke Iordanescu’s appointment sounds like a match made in heaven.

For Hornets fans, though, it’s an act of desperation from a club that has no plan, structure or hope.

In truth, Dionisi is the latest in a series of head coaches who have been let down by owner Pozzo, chairman Scott Duxbury and technical director Gianluca Nani, who seem incapable of building a squad or supporting a head coach.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Things could have been so different for the Italian, because at the start of the season, there was clearly something there. Watford were excellent in their opening day win over Southampton - playing with real flair and intensity in the first half - and followed that up with draws against Wrexham and West Ham. It was clear the players respected the Italian.

It has been revealed that however, the warning signs were already there. In the summer, Dionisi and supporters were told that Watford would prioritise experienced players in the transfer market. None arrived.

Nestory Irankunda, Imran Louza and Giorgi Chakvetadze - three key players - were sold and not replaced, with Watford starting the season with just two centre-backs on the club’s books and two fit central midfielders.

Recent findings suggest that the Italian sounded increasingly exasperated as his calls for reinforcements fell on deaf ears until the final few days of the window, where Watford eventually panicked and brought in Stephy Mavididi, Soumaila Coulibaly and Branimir Mlacic on loan. Myron Boadu and Michail Antonio arrived on free transfers.

Most of those players arrived unfit and come September, Dionisi was struggling to fill the bench as injuries took hold. The Italian never really recovered from embarrassing defeats to Burnley and Cardiff City, deploying a back five in recent weeks as he attempted to make the Golden Boys harder to beat.

Quite frankly, Watford are unmanageable. Not even Pep Guardiola would be successful at Vicarage Road, because no head coach is given the opportunity to implement a style of play when they have to contend with poor recruitment, a leadership vacuum and a dressing room with seemingly poor attitudes.

Rob Edwards was promised he'd be backed in the transfer market come hell or high water by chairman Duxbury in the summer of 2022. Most of the signings he received didn't fit his system and he was sacked within two months of the season starting.

Industry observers note that after Edwards, Slaven Bilic thought he'd be able to sign players he wanted in the January transfer window. He received Joao Ferreira and Henrique Araujo - both of whom never looked suited to Championship football – as well as Ryan Porteous, Wesley Hoedt and Britt Assombalonga. Bilic was gone by March.

In a recent development, then came Chris Wilder, who repeatedly called out the poor attitude within the dressing room and wasn't given a contract extension when his deal expired in the summer of 2023. After the wheels came off under Valerian Ismael, Tom Cleverley was promoted to head coach in 2024 and despite a thin squad, united the players and fans, having been a popular player at Vicarage Road during his playing days.

Once again, though, January arrived and Cleverley didn't get the options he so dearly needed, meaning Watford's form dropped off and he was sacked, somewhat harshly, at the end of the season.

Just last season, the popular Javi Gracia returned for a second spell in charge and had Watford in the play-off spots by January. He was promised additions, but none were forthcoming and ultimately the Spaniard decided the job wasn't worth his time. Gracia resigned, returning to Spain to spend time with his family.

Recent findings suggest that in short, it's time the Watford ownership took a long, hard look at themselves, rather than the head coach. Has Iordanescu been appointed because no one sensible will take it? Any head coach worth his salt in England - and possibly now Italy, too - knows what they’re walking into.

Industry observers note that in a recent interview with Roy Moore from the 1881 Movement, Pozzo tried shifting accountability for the club’s downfall, which can be traced back to the FA Cup Final in 2019. Since then, numerous decisions have, in the eyes of supporters, led to the erosion of the club's identity - fans have had enough.

Empty statements, the constant churn of players and head coaches, and what appears to be a lack of any real structure or strategy - supporters are fed up.

The fact Watford closed their Under-21 setup, downgraded their academy and sold off the women's team this summer was a huge source of disappointment for fans, too, given the club’s rich history of bringing players through their youth system.

Unless there is a sudden change of approach overnight, Watford are only heading one way and that's down to League 1.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 10:49 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 12:07 EST, 27 November 2026.
  • Gary Neville has claimed he is 'absolutely certain' Erling Haaland will leave Manchester City for Real Madrid within the next 18 months amid the impact of their legal battle with the Premier League.
  • Haaland has cut a despondent figure in recent weeks following Man City's underwhelming run of form.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By MICHAEL PAVITT, SPORTS REPORTER.

Published: 10:49 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 12:07 EST, 27 November 2026.

Gary Neville has claimed he is 'absolutely certain' Erling Haaland will leave Manchester City for Real Madrid within the next 18 months amid the impact of their legal battle with the Premier League.

Haaland has cut a despondent figure in recent weeks following Man City's underwhelming run of form.

The Norwegian star admitted to 'questioning everything' after their 2-2 draw against Napoli in the Champions League in midweek, while Man City fans expressed concerns over Haaland's downbeat assessment and body language.

The result meant City have won just twice in their last seven matches – one of which was achieved in a penalty shoot-out against Brighton in the Carabao Cup.

Man City have suffered defeats to Aston Villa, Brighton and Nottingham Forest in the Premier League in the run, as well as drawing with Fulham on the weekend.

In a recent development, neville, speaking on the Overlap, suggested the mood at Man City may have been affected in recent weeks after the club were found guilty of the vast majority of charges brought against them by the Premier League for financial wrongdoing. Man City have since appealed the decision.

Gary Neville has mentioned he is 'absolutely certain' Erling Haaland will leave Manchester City for Real Madrid within the next 18 months.

Neville suggested Haaland's spell at Man City could be coming to an end after questioning whether the 'cloud' of the Premier League charges verdict has impacted the mood at the club.

The former Man United defender theorised that Haaland's time at the club could be coming to an end and that he expects the forward to join Real Madrid in the near future.

'It feels like something has changed in these last few weeks with City, it feels like maybe that mood, that cloud, is just starting to [impact],' Neville noted.

'I don't think Haaland is going to be here, I think he will be at Real Madrid in the next, maximum 18 months, maybe even at the end of the season.

'I can see Vinicius leaving, I can see Mbappe going a bit to the left and Haaland going up there [down the middle].

'If you look at Florentino Perez, he goes and signs the best strikers in the world, the best players in the world.

'I just think because of what has happened to City, I think Haaland is going to Real Madrid.

'I am absolutely certain he will be in a Real Madrid shirt in the next 18 months.'.

It had long been viewed that Haaland's career proposal had involved moving to LaLiga, with Real Madrid long-term admirers.

Real Madrid have held a long-standing interest in the Manchester City superstar.

Neville claimed Real Madrid president Florentino Perez could opt to sell Vinicius Jr before moving for Haaland.

The forward, however, signed a nine-and-a-half-year deal in early 2025, taking his Man City contract through to 2034.

Haaland had pushed back against suggestions the case had affected their form during the international break, while stressing he was committed long-term to the club.

The forward's first answer to Norwegian broadcaster TV2 had spanned two minutes and 14 seconds, as he reeled off the teams he had represented from 2009 to 2018, the years covered by the charges after he was asked about the club's situation.

'In 2009, I played for Bryne U9s. In 2010, the U10s. In 2011, the U11s. 2012, the U12s, 2013, the U13s. Shall we continue? We don't need the whole list. 2014, the U14s. 2015, the U15s and the national team,' Haaland noted.

In a recent development, 'Then the U16s, I think. In 2016, I moved up to Bryne's first team, second team and youth team. In 2017, I went to Molde. In 2018, I was with Molde. The first team, Molde 2 and a bit with the youth team.

'So this is a question I struggle to answer because it's a legal battle….

'It's a case between the Premier League and Manchester City that a panel will deal with. Am I supposed to answer that? I'm not really sure.'.

Haaland cut a despondent figure in midweek as he admitted to 'questioning everything' after Man City's draw with Napoli continued their underwhelming form.

Haaland has pushed back against suggestions the Premier League charges verdict has had an impact on Man City's form.

He continued: 'It's a difficult question to answer when I don't really know that much about it.

Sources indicate that 'I assume the answers will come… I don't know when. I haven't read much about it.

'To be completely honest, I'm focused on trying to perform for Manchester City.'.

Haaland, who has scored 176 goals in 214 appearances for Man City, will be hoping to spark Enzo Maresca's side back into form when they face Premier League leaders Arsenal on Sunday.

Arsenal are currently six points clear of Man City heading into the match as they bid to retain their title this season.

#151313. The haunting Masters meltdown that changed Rory McIlroy's career

📅 03 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1596 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNN ↗ Open Full Page

The haunting Masters meltdown that changed Rory McIlroy's career

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1596 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Editor’s Note:  This story was originally published in April 2023.
  • Slumped on his club, head buried in his arm, Rory McIlroy looked on the verge of tears.
  • The then-21-year-old had just watched his ball sink into the waters of Rae’s Creek at Augusta National and with it, his dream of winning The Masters, a dream that had looked so tantalizingly close mere hours earlier.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s Note:  This story was originally published in April 2023.

Slumped on his club, head buried in his arm, Rory McIlroy looked on the verge of tears.

The then-21-year-old had just watched his ball sink into the waters of Rae’s Creek at Augusta National and with it, his dream of winning The Masters, a dream that had looked so tantalizingly close mere hours earlier.

As a four-time major winner and one of the most decorated names in the sport’s history, few players would turn down the chance to swap places with McIlroy heading into Augusta this week.

Yet on Sunday afternoon of April 10, 2011, not a golfer in the world would have wished to be in the Northern Irishman’s shoes.

A fresh-faced, mop-headed McIlroy had touched down in Georgia for the first major of the season with a reputation as the leading light of the next generation of stars.

An excellent 2010 had marked his best season since turning pro three years earlier, highlighted by a first PGA Tour win at the Quail Hollow Championship and a crucial contribution to Team Europe’s triumph at the Ryder Cup.

Yet despite a pair of impressive top-three finishes at the Open and PGA Championship respectively, a disappointing missed cut at The Masters – his first at a major – served as ominous foreshadowing.

McIlroy shot 74 and 77 to fall four strokes short of the cut line at seven-over par, a performance that concerned him enough to take a brief sabbatical from competition.

But one year on in 2011, any lingering Masters demons looked to have been exorcised as McIlroy flew round the Augusta fairways.

Having opened with a bogey-free seven-under 65 – the first time he had ever shot in the 60s at the major – McIlroy pulled ahead from Spanish first round co-leader Alvaro Quirós with a second round 69.

It sent him into the weekend holding a two-shot cushion over Australia’s Jason Day, with Tiger Woods a further stroke behind and back in the hunt for a 15th major after a surging second round 66.

And yet the 21-year-old leader looked perfectly at ease with having a target on his back. Even after a tentative start to the third round, McIlroy rallied with three birdies across the closing six holes to stretch his lead to four strokes heading into Sunday.

The youngster was out on his own ahead of a bunched chasing pack comprising Day, Ángel Cabrera, K.J. Choi and Charl Schwartzel. After 54 holes, McIlroy had shot just three bogeys.

“It’s a great position to be in … I’m finally feeling comfortable on this golf course,” McIlroy told reporters.

Recent findings suggest that “I’m not getting ahead of myself, I know how leads can dwindle away very swiftly. I have to go out there, not take anything for granted and go out and play as hard as I’ve played the last three days. If I can do that, hopefully things will go my way.

“We’ll see what happens tomorrow because four shots on this golf course isn’t that much.”.

The truth can hurt, and McIlroy was about to prove his assessment of Augusta to be true in the most excruciating way imaginable.

His fourth bogey of the week arrived immediately. Having admitted to expecting some nerves at the first tee, McIlroy sparked a booming opening drive down the fairway, only to miss his putt from five feet.

In a recent development, three consecutive pars steadied the ship, but Schwartzel had the wind in his sails. A blistering birdie, par, eagle start had seen him draw level at the summit after his third hole.

A subsequent bogey from the South African slowed his charge, as McIlroy clung onto a one-shot lead at the turn from Schwartzel, Cabrera, Choi, and a rampaging Woods, who shot five birdies and an eagle across the front nine to send Augusta into a frenzy.

Despite his dwindling advantage and the raucous Tiger-mania din ahead of him, McIlroy had responded well to another bogey at the 5th hole, draining a brilliant 20-foot putt at the 7th to restore his lead.

The fist pump that followed marked the high-water point of McIlroy’s round, as a sliding start accelerated into full-blown free-fall at the par-four 10th hole.

His tee shot went careening into a tree, ricocheting to settle between the white cabins that separate the main course from the adjacent par-three course. It offered viewers a glimpse at a part of Augusta rarely seen on broadcast, followed by pictures of McIlroy anxiously peering out from behind a tree to track his follow-up shot.

In a recent development, though his initial escape was successful, yet another collision with a tree and a two-putt on the green saw a stunned McIlroy eventually tap in for a triple bogey. Having led the field one hole and seven shots earlier, he arrived at the 11th tee in seventh.

By the time his tee drive at the 13th plopped into the creek, all thoughts of who might be the recipient of the green jacket had long-since switched away from the anguished youngster. It had taken him seven putts to navigate the previous two greens, as a bogey and a double bogey dropped him to five-under – the score he had held after just 11 holes of the tournament.

According to recent reports, mercifully, the last five holes passed without major incident. A missed putt for birdie from five feet at the final hole summed up McIlroy’s day, though he was given a rousing reception as he left the green.

Mere minutes earlier, the same crowd had erupted as Schwartzel sunk his fourth consecutive birdie to seal his first major title. After starting the day four shots adrift of McIlroy, the South African finished 10 shots ahead of him, and two ahead of second-placed Australian duo Jason Day and Adam Scott.

McIlroy’s eight-over 80 marked the highest score of the round. Having headlined the leaderboard for most of the week, he finished tied-15th.

Tears would flow during a phone call with his parents the following morning, but at his press conference, McIlroy was upbeat.

“I’m very disappointed at the minute, and I’m sure I will be for the next few days, but I’ll get over it,” he remarked.

“I was leading this golf tournament with nine holes to go, and I just unraveled … It’s a Sunday at a major, what it can do.

“This is my first experience at it, and hopefully the next time I’m in this position I’ll be able to handle it a little better. I didn’t handle it particularly well today obviously, but it was a character-building day … I’ll come out stronger for it.”.

Once again, McIlroy would be proven right.

Industry observers note that just eight weeks later in June, McIlroy rampaged to an eight-shot victory at the US Open. Records tumbled in his wake at Congressional, as he shot a tournament record 16-under 268 to become the youngest major winner since Tiger Woods at The Masters in 1997.

Sources indicate that the historic victory kickstarted a golden era for McIlroy. After coasting to another eight-shot win at the PGA Championship in 2012, McIlroy became only the third golfer since 1934 to win three majors by the age of 25 with triumph at the 2014 Open Championship.

Before the year was out, he would add his fourth major title with another PGA Championship win.

Sources indicate that and much of it was owed to that fateful afternoon at Augusta. In an interview with the BBC in 2015, McIlroy dubbed it “the most vital day” of his career.

“If I had not had the whole unravelling, if I had just made a couple of bogeys coming down the stretch and lost by one, I would not have learned as much.

According to recent reports, “Luckily, it did not take me long to get into a position like that again when I was leading a major and I was able to get over the line quite comfortably. It was a huge learning curve for me and I needed it, and thankfully I have been able to move on to bigger and better things.

“Looking back on what happened in 2011, it doesn’t seem as bad when you have four majors on your mantelpiece.”.

McIlroy’s contentment came with a caveat: it would be “unthinkable” if he did not win The Masters in his career.

Yet as he prepares for his 15th appearance at Augusta National this week, a green jacket remains an elusive missing item from his wardrobe.

Despite seven top-10 finishes in his past 10 Masters outings, the trophy remains the only thing separating McIlroy from joining the ranks of golf immortals to have completed golf’s career grand slam of all four majors in the modern era: Gene Sarazen, Ben Hogan, Gary Player, Jack Nicklaus, and Tiger Woods.

A runner-up finish to Scottie Scheffler last year marked McIlroy’s best finish at Augusta, yet arguably 2011 remains the closest he has ever been to victory. A slow start in 2022 meant McIlroy had begun Sunday’s deciding round 10 shots adrift of the American, who teed off for his final hole with a five-shot lead despite McIlroy’s brilliant 64 finish.

Rory McIlroy: I will win the Masters.

At 33 years old, time is still on his side. Though 2022 extended his major drought to eight years, it featured arguably his best golf since that golden season in 2014.

And as McIlroy knows better than most, things can change quickly at Augusta National.

The summer that changed Welsh football

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Wales had gone more than half a century without playing at a major tournament, so it was understandable that expectations were modest.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Walking to the ground in Bordeaux and what I find hilarious, in hindsight, is how low our expectations were.".

Wales had gone more than half a century without playing at a major tournament, so it was understandable that expectations were modest.

Generations of fans had been scarred by agonising near misses and downright dismal failures of the past so, when Wales finally realised a nation's dream by qualifying for Euro 2016, just being there was enough for many.

Bordeaux was bathed in sunshine on the afternoon of Saturday, 11 June, tens of thousands of Welsh supporters descending on the French city for their opening game against Slovakia.

"We were all saying things like, 'Oh, the anthem's going to be good, that's guaranteed'. We could have lost 10-0 but they were definitely playing the anthem," the comedian and presenter tells BBC Sport Wales as part of Iconic: The Summer that Changed Welsh Football.

Sources indicate that an anthem heard at a major tournament for the first time in 58 years. Glorious catharsis to stir the soul.

Wales had ridden a wave of emotion to get there, a golden generation of players - Gareth Bale, Aaron Ramsey et al - scaling latest heights under the guidance of their charismatic manager Chris Coleman.

"I was saying to all the players, 'Keep calm, don't act like we're too excited to be here'," Coleman recalls.

"But Bordeaux was like the centre of Cardiff, Welsh fans everywhere outside the hotel and, as soon as we were getting on the bus, I was chanting with the fans! I was like, 'What am I doing? Calm down'. I got lost in it.".

In a recent development, coleman and his players eventually composed themselves. After a trademark Bale free-kick had put Wales in front, Hal Robson-Kanu came off the bench to score a late winner and send a nation into raptures.

"Euro 2016 was a turning point for Welsh football," says Ben Davies, the Tottenham Hotspur defender who made a crucial goalline block early in the game.

"There was so much talk about 1958 and I'd heard about it, I'd seen the odd clip about it, but it felt like a pipedream to actually have Wales in a major tournament.

"So to do it, forget about how well we did in it, just to even get to that tournament, it gave us a belief that it was possible.".

For those among the sea of red shirts in Bordeaux that day, it did not feel like life could get any better - but this was only the beginning.

This was the summer that would change Welsh football forever.

âIt was like being in the centre of Cardiff â there were Welsh fans everywhereâ.

Until Euro 2016, Wales' story had been dominated by tales of heartache, Joe Jordan's handball in 1977 and the Romania defeat of 1993 among many painful chapters.

But by getting to France, Wales freed themselves from that history.

"There had been some really low points for Wales, so to finally do that was a huge achievement," says Ramsey, the then Arsenal midfielder who would go on to be named in Uefa's team of the tournament.

Wales had momentum they had never felt before coming into the competition. Victory over Slovakia - and the prospect of getting to the second round - took that to another level.

A last-gasp defeat by England in Lens momentarily punctured that optimism, but the final group game against Russia presented Coleman's side with a chance to secure their place in the knockout stages.

This was meant to be nerve-wracking for a team with no major tournament experience against seasoned opponents.

But under a lilac sunset in Toulouse, Coleman's men played with a flair and verve unlike any other Wales side.

In a recent development, "That was our best performance," says Coleman. "We were awesome.".

Wales cut Russia to ribbons with a breathtaking attacking display, racing into a 2-0 lead in 20 minutes.

After Ramsey's delicate finish put Wales in front, they poured forward with such gusto that even Neil Taylor scored - the wing-back's first goal since he was playing in non-league for Wrexham six years earlier.

"When Tayls scored, that summed up how things were falling for us," notes Joe Allen, who was exceptional in midfield that night.

"This was one of those once-in-a-lifetime moments you've got to capitalise on.".

It has been revealed that that is exactly what Wales did. Bale added a third in the second half to become the tournament's top scorer at that point, and the winning margin could have been even wider.

Joe Ledley (right) dances in front of the Wales fans after the 3-0 win over Russia in Toulouse.

"We completely dominated them," indicates Joe Ledley, who ran the game alongside Allen in midfield.

As well as Ledley played, though, what elevated him to cult status was his post-match dancing in front of the Wales fans.

"I don't know where those moves came from," he grins. "I used to dance with my mates all the time at local pubs in Fairwater [in Cardiff]. I just went for it.".

Sources indicate that wales fans could scarcely believe what they had witnessed. Having already lived a dreamlike existence in France, this was starting to feel surreal.

The odyssey took them to Paris next, Wales' first knockout fixture since Pele had scored the only goal as Brazil beat them in a 1958 World Cup quarter-final.

This time, Coleman's men had the novelty of being favourites against an obdurate Northern Ireland side, who made life difficult for their opponents in a tense last-16 tie.

Bale eventually prised them open â his cross turned into his own net by Gareth McAuley â to set up a quarter-final against Belgium, and what would turn out to be the greatest night in Welsh football history.

'I remember like it was yesterday' - Euro 2016 hero Robson-Kanu.

Wales fans made a lasting impression in France, with their distinctive bucket hats and chant of 'Don't Take Me Home', which became an unofficial anthem of the Euros. Uefa even gave them an "outstanding contribution" award.

"What I loved about Welsh supporters at the Euros was we were just desperate to enjoy every second and suck the marrow out of it because we didn't know if it was going to happen again," notes James.

Sources indicate that "We're there to have fun. I'm not saying the result was secondary, but we all had realistic expectations.".

No wonder when you consider Wales' quarter-final opponents were Belgium, ranked number one in the world at the time with a squad boasting stellar talents such as Kevin de Bruyne, Romelu Lukaku and Eden Hazard.

"That Belgian side, on paper, was like a team to represent Earth against Mars," James adds. "It was like a team from space.".

It did not help matters that the game was essentially a home fixture for Belgium, whose fans filled the stadium in Lille, fewer than 10 miles from the Belgian border.

The odds were stacked against Coleman and his players, lengthening further when Radja Nainggolan's thunderous long-range strike gave Belgium an early lead.

But Wales believed they could win, not least because they had beaten Belgium in a qualifier in Cardiff 13 months earlier, and they responded magnificently as captain Ashley Williams headed in a deserved equaliser.

Then, nine minutes into the second half, Bale played a raking long ball to Ramsey, who found Robson-Kanu in the penalty area. And time stood still.

"I remember controlling the ball in the box and there was momentum carrying everyone away from the goal," Robson-Kanu says. "I just remember Cruyffing the entire opposition.".

With a manoeuvre as audacious as it was inspired, Robson-Kanu flummoxed three surrounding Belgian defenders with a Cruyff-turn before finishing supremely beyond Thibaut Courtois.

Wales' fans came to be known as the Red Wall during Euro 2016.

"It was an out-of-body experience," adds the forward, who was without a club at the time.

"Looking back, you realise careers are defined by moments, and to have a moment that you're truly remembered for is a real honour.".

Recent findings suggest that belgium pushed desperately for an equaliser but Sam Vokes headed in superbly to seal a 3-1 triumph. The celebrations were as ecstatic on the touchline as they were in the stands; disbelief as it dawned on players, staff and fans that Wales were heading to their first semi-final.

"There are certain moments in your life that are so good you wish you could just stop it and say, 'Let's just sit in this moment'," claims Coleman.

"That was one of those moments. We got back in the dressing room and I can't describe the atmosphere.".

Allen, another Welshman in Uefa's team of the tournament, adds: "That's the moment where it crossed from being a good story into, 'This is more than anyone dreamed was possible'.".

The next, and what would prove to be the final, stop on Wales' magical ride was a semi-final against eventual champions Portugal in Lyon.

Shorn of the suspended Ramsey and Davies, Wales were stifled by their canny opponents, who secured a 2-0 win with second-half goals from Cristiano Ronaldo and Nani.

This was the end of the adventure in France, but the beginning of a glorious era for Welsh football.

"It was a really crucial moment for Wales, our history and generations to come," says Ramsey.

Having been absent from major tournaments for 58 years, Wales went on to qualify for a second successive European Championship, before achieving what Davies describes as the "holy grail" of reaching a first World Cup for 64 years in 2022.

"We opened the door that had been closed a long time," notes Coleman.

The milestones kept coming, with the women's side qualifying for their first major tournament at Euro 2025.

Whereas Welsh national teams only used to dream of playing on the world's grandest stages, there is now an expectation they get there â and that stems from 2016.

Wales players and staff celebrate with their fans after their Euro 2016 quarter-final win over Belgium.

"With more money coming in from qualification for the European Championships, particularly Euro 2016, we ended up being more cash-rich," claims Jonathan Ford, chief executive of the Football Association of Wales (FAW) from 2009 to 2021.

It has been revealed that "That enabled us to put more money across the board: women's football, grassroots football. We transformed the women's game.".

Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister is a former captain of Wales who played a leading role in getting the FAW to formally establish a national women's team in the 1990s.

"There was nothing inevitable about what happened post-2016 and that's why I think we should give credit to the FAW, and Jonathan Ford particularly, for steering us out of the tournament into that era," notes McAllister.

"I was part of the FAW Trust in 2016. I can remember times before that when Jonathan came into the board and remarked things like, 'Until the men qualify for a major tournament, we can't invest in X, Y and Z'. And that included the women's national team.

"While I bristled at that because it felt unfair, the financial realities of the FAW meant until the men got to a position where they generated income from participating and winning, it was going to be impossible for us to deliver the strategy we had for Welsh football.".

McAllister travelled to France 10 years ago as a fan, and Qatar in 2022 to cheer on Wales' men at a World Cup.

When the women played at Euro 2025 in Switzerland, McAllister was there again to see the legacy not only of her own pioneering work in establishing the team but the far-reaching effects of 2016.

Industry observers note that "Something happens when you qualify. It's flicking a switch in mentality - it becomes something realistic and achievable," she adds.

"What matters far more is what you do with the breakthrough moment, not how you've performed.".

Wales' women are now trying to take the next step of qualifying for their first World Cup, while the men looked on enviously as their showpiece event happened without them in the United States, Canada and Mexico this summer.

Disappointing as it was, that frustration itself represented a shift in mindset that came after Euro 2016 â a sharp contrast to the passive acceptance that met Wales' previous absence from major tournaments.

Since that golden month in France, Wales feel like they belong at this level.

"The best thing we could give the teams coming after us was to say it's possible," says Coleman.

Subsequent qualifications have been the legacy of Euro 2016, while future ambitions are proof of a desire to ensure generations to come continue to build on the foundations laid by their predecessors.

There is plenty more Wales' men and women want to achieve but, whatever happens, there will never be another summer quite like Euro 2016.

"We're so proud of each other and what we achieved," says Ledley.

"Nobody thought we'd do it. When I walk down the street now, everyone says, 'Thank you for 2016, the best summer of my life'.".

Recent findings suggest that james can attest to that. "It remains the best month of my life," he says. "I don't think you often know it's the best month of your life as it's happening.".

With the benefit of hindsight, it is laughable to think you could find a Welsh football fan who would disagree.

In a recent development, never be the man after ‘the man’, the saying goes. Football history is stippled with cautionary tales of managers who followed an all-time great, only to discover that they were doomed from the very beginning.

According to recent reports, manchester City have stumbled through a bruising autumn under Enzo Maresca, uncharacteristically so. It is impossible not to wonder if the Etihad Stadium is experiencing its very own version of Manchester United's 2013/14.

For a decade, Pep Guardiola bent English football to his will, turning Man City into a relentless, trophy-winning machine. Succeeding a figure who loomed so large over the east side of Manchester was never going to be straightforward. Few, though, expected the drop-off to feel quite so jarring, or quite so familiar.

David Moyes arrived at Old Trafford in 2013 tasked with prolonging Sir Alex Ferguson’s dynasty, meanwhile Maresca was handed a three-year contract this summer to keep Guardiola’s juggernaut in motion. Four months into the job, the steering wheel is juddering uncomfortably.

In a recent development, man City’s recent results make for grim reading compared to the standards set over the last 10 years. A 3-1 defeat away at Nottingham Forest earlier this month was double-take worthy, before Saturday’s 1-1 home draw with Fulham - rescued only by an Elliot Anderson volley - saw them lose yet more ground in the Premier League title race.

On Tuesday night in the Champions League, Man City needed an 86th-minute Rayan Cherki strike just to salvage a 2-2 draw at home to Napoli, right now eighth in Serie A and 14 points off the pace.

Ahead of Sunday’s trip to league leaders Arsenal, Maresca's men look a shadow of the team that so recently struck fear into the Gunners' title hopes.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Predictably, the question of Maresca’s future has already begun to take on more of a 'when rather than if' feel. Reports emerged this week suggesting the Italian is fighting to save his job barely a third of the way into his debut Etihad campaign. Sack talk at Manchester City circulating at all, never mind in November, speaks volumes about how rapidly things have changed.

There are parallels between Man City’s recent slump and Moyes’ 10-month spell across town, too. Like Moyes, Maresca inherited a squad undergoing significant churn after an era of dominance.

To bridge that gap, City made a throng of massive summer purchases, bringing in additions such as Elliot Anderson, Enzo Fernandez, Iliman Ndiaye and Ayyoub Bouaddi.

Much like Moyes’ integration of Marouane Fellaini and Juan Mata into a fading champion side, Maresca’s fresh-look Man City feels disjointed - caught between Guardiola’s positional automatisms and a new manager’s attempt to stamp his own authority on the dressing room.

That disconnect quickly becomes apparent when the team aren't getting results, breeding doubt among players accustomed to certainty and success. All of which begs the question: was Maresca always doomed to fail?

In a recent development, following Guardiola was always going to be an exercise in managing impossible expectations while rebuilding in real time. Perhaps the Etihad hierarchy believed their structure would insulate Guardiola’s successor from the same sort of post-Ferguson collapse that swallowed Moyes' efforts - which in hindsight weren't all that bad. Perhaps there is a lesson there for Man City chiefs to heed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sixteen-year-old Summer McIntosh broke the world record for the 400m individual medley at the Canadian swimming trials on Saturday – just days after breaking the world record for the 400m freestyle.

McIntosh finished the 400m individual medley in a time of 4:25.87, breaking the mark set at the 2016 Rio Olympics by Hungarian swimmer Katinka Hosszú with a time of 4:26.36.

The result continues the teenager’s brilliant week after she broke the 400m freestyle world record last Tuesday – breaking defending Olympic champion Ariarne Titmus’ previous record of 3:56.40, which was set last May, in a time of 3:56.08.

Speaking after her latest triumph, McIntosh shared her emotions.

“That’s the first time I really vividly heard the crowd during my race,” McIntosh noted, per Reuters.

It has been revealed that “It’s amazing to have all my family and friends in the stands, cheering me on. It really helped me in the last 100 meters.”.

The Canadian teen made her Olympic debut aged 14 at Tokyo 2020, where she finished fourth in the 200-meter freestyle.

She bagged gold in the 200m butterfly and 400m medley at the world championships in 2022, as well as two golds at the Commonwealth Games in the 200m and 400m medleys.

She now trains in Florida under coach Brent Arckey with the Sarasota Sharks team.
