The Europa League game between Besiktas and Israel's Hapoel Beer-Sheva was suspended for around 30 minutes on Thursday when police clashed with fans of the Turkish club after they displayed a banner in support of Palestine.

The game, being played on neutral ground in Batumi, Georgia, was halted in the 26th minute but restarted after the interruption.

Turkey’s Haberturk broadcaster said Georgian police used pepper spray against the Besiktas fans, who also unfurled a Palestinian flag, prompting referee referee Morten Krogh to stop the game with the score 0-0.

Besiktas went on to win the game 2-1.

In a statement, Besiktas accused the Georgian security forces of using “disproportionate” force against supporters before and during the game.

Georgian police entered the stands and ⁠used pepper spray on Besiktas fans, Turkish outlet NTV reported.

“We strongly condemn the security forces for their use of disproportionate force against our fans,” the club said. “We also extend our best wishes for a speedy recovery to all our fans affected by these incidents.”.

The report added that Turkish fans chanted “Down with Israel” and that Besiktas players and director of football Onder Ozen spoke to supporters before play restarted to calm the situation.

The Turkish Football Federation condemned the treatment of Besiktas supporters on X, saying they were subjected to unacceptable behaviour and discrimination. It said it would press for an investigation.

The TFF’s statement read: “We strongly condemn the unacceptable attitudes, conduct and interference directed at Beşiktaş supporters, both inside and outside the stadium, before and during our club’s Uefa Europa League match against Hapoel Beer-Sheva in Georgia.

“No practice that disregards the universal values of sport, human dignity, mutual respect and the principles of fair play, or that involves discrimination, exclusion or security failures, can be tolerated.

“Nor can there be any question of remaining silent in the face of such conduct, which endangers our supporters’ safety and targets their fundamental rights and freedoms.

“As the Turkish Football Federation, we declare unequivocally that we will follow this matter to its conclusion to ensure that the events are fully investigated, those responsible are identified and the necessary sanctions are imposed without delay.

“There must be no tolerance for covering up these events, allowing those responsible to evade accountability or permitting similar violations to recur.

“We emphasize that we stand firmly with our club, Besiktas, and our supporters, who faced a series of problems, particularly serious security failures, and extend our best wishes for a speedy recovery to all our supporters subjected to interference and mistreatment.

“Let no one forget that we will not remain silent in the face of disrespect, discrimination and security violations directed at representatives and supporters of Turkish football.

“We will act decisively on national and international platforms to ensure that all necessary steps are taken, particularly with Uefa, and that those responsible are held accountable.”.

Turkish clubs echoed the sentiments of the TFF, with Besiktas’ rivals Fenerbahce, Galatasaray and Trabzonspor all among those to stand with the club.

“We do not accept Turkish clubs being denied the right to play their home matches in their own country, in front of their own fans, when facing clubs from the occupying state of Israel,” Trabzonspor wrote in a statement.

Industry observers note that “We do not consider Uefa’s double standards on this glitch acceptable. We also strongly condemn the disproportionate intervention by security forces against Besiktas fans in Georgia this evening.”.

The ⁠officiating team and the Besiktas players ‌left ​the pitch before ‌the game restarted.

Earlier, the Besiktas players refused to shake hands with their Hapoel counterparts, the state-run Anadolu Agency reported.

Hapoel Beer-Sheva and Israel FA had not commented on the incident at the time of publishing.

#151214. German directors' doc on stolen film wins International Emmy Award

📅 24 Feb 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1060 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

German directors' doc on stolen film wins International Emmy Award

📅 24 Feb 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1060 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it sounds like the plot of a screenplay, but it happened to two Berlin film students in real life.
  • Moritz Henneberg and Julius Drost had created an animated short film for their final project at university.
  • "Butty" tells the tale of a household robot that gets kicked out when it can't do its job properly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it sounds like the plot of a screenplay, but it happened to two Berlin film students in real life. The documentary they made out of their unusual story, "The Talented Mr. F," has now won an International Emmy Award.

Moritz Henneberg and Julius Drost had created an animated short film for their final project at university.

"Butty" tells the tale of a household robot that gets kicked out when it can't do its job properly.

Industry observers note that when the two filmmakers posted the work on YouTube, this touching tale promptly went viral. After generating a huge amount of hits, the duo decided to submit their work to festivals — but they were in for a shock: Organizers told them the film had already been submitted under a different name.

US student Samuel Felinton downloaded the film, made minimal edits, gave it a new title, "T-130," and removed the original credits. As the alleged author, he went on to win numerous prizes and made a name for himself in the United States.

It has been revealed that shocked by the blatant theft of their work, Henneberg and Drost sought legal advice. They were told that if they opted to sue, the process would be arduous and costly. So, the filmmakers took matters into their own hands and went to the US to confront Felinton — filming their journey along the way.

Recent findings suggest that "We'd already made documentary films," Henneberg told DW. "And the idea just popped into our heads: This is a brilliant story — let's make a documentary about it.".

The two directors had developed a kind of fascination for the man who'd stolen their film.

Sources indicate that "We looked at his vlogs and sort of took a deep dive into his world," remarked Drost. "We almost saw him as a kind of celebrity. We discovered a lot about him and really wanted to meet him in person.".

Sources indicate that while family and friends reacted with anger, the two young filmmakers remained surprisingly calm. They were more perplexed than anything: "Our families and friends hated Samuel. But we just wanted to understand what had happened," they stated.

The pair put together a film crew and traveled to Morgantown, West Virginia — the university town where Felinton lives. With the help of a Newly introduced York filmmaker pretending to make a documentary about young animators, they won Felinton's trust — and then Henneberg, Drost and Felinton were finally in a room together.

Sources indicate that the two German filmmakers had prepared for all manner of scenarios ahead of the meeting: "We expected an emotional reaction — that he'd run away, cry, be ashamed or get aggressive. But he remained completely calm. That was the only thing we hadn't bargained for. We thought his world would implode. But he showed barely any emotion at all," they recalled.

According to recent reports, felinton explained how he'd shortened and "improved" the film and that this was how it became such a success. He agreed to transfer any prize money. His manner was cool and matter-of-fact, which Drost and Henneberg found both unsettling and fascinating. After their chat, the three barbecued together and played a round of basketball.

Industry observers note that later, many viewers accused the two German filmmakers of being too soft on the plagiarist. Others praised their approach.

"The reactions were very divided," remarked Drost. "Some said we should've sued him or punched him in the face. Others said we'd shown new ways to resolve conflicts.".

Industry observers note that "And in the end, it wasn't personal," added Henneberg. "He wanted to make something of himself — he could've taken another film. But if a big studio like Pixar had stolen our film, that'd be quite a different story.".

And so, Henneberg and Drost made the conscious decision to keep things respectful.

They didn't want to "publicly embarrass him or punish him any more than necessary," they said, adding that their documentary was sufficient "revenge.".

Recent findings suggest that the title of the documentary, "Der talentierte Mister F." ("The Talented Mister F."), is no coincidence. It's a play on the movie title "The Talented Mr. Ripley," the story of a young man who assumes the identity of a wealthy heir and ends up mired in a web of lies, fraud and, finally, murder. And just like Mr. Ripley, Felinton had also assumed a false identity.

Felinton did actually end up sending them the trophies he had won, as well as a sum of money.

Sources indicate that for their part, however, the festivals preferred to keep their distance from the saga. As one organizer said: The prize has been awarded, and there's nothing we can do about it — it's up to these guys to work things out between themselves.

Recent findings suggest that for the original filmmakers themselves, the scandal has also had a positive impact: Since the documentary was released in Germany in October 2025, their animation film has garnered even more attention on YouTube. Henneberg and Drost uploaded it again, and in the credits, special thanks also go out to Samuel Felinton.

And now, the documentary is winning its own awards: Before being honored with the International Emmy Award, it also won a Grimme Prize, one of Germany's most prestigious television awards.

Felinton was able to steal the film in the first place in part because when it first appeared online in 2023, it could just be downloaded from YouTube.

Drost and Henneberg say uploading "Butty" back then wasn't a mistake, saying that was the risk of putting something online.

The alternative would have been not to show the film at all, they said; then no one would have seen it.

They have a clear message for young creatives.

"Don't be discouraged. Be aware that something like this can happen — but stay creative in how you deal with it. Suing is expensive and often doesn't do much good. Instead, show the world that you're the authors.".

What started out as film plagiarism ended up becoming material for another project. And that's perhaps the most unusual twist in this very quirky story.

This article was originally published in German in February 2026 and was updated on November 24, 2026, following the International Emmy Awards.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, some VIP Twitter consumers woke up on Saturday expecting to have lost their coveted blue verification check marks in a previously declared purge by Elon Musk.
  • In a recent development, twitter had said it would “begin winding down” blue checks granted under its old verification system — which emphasized protecting high-profile users at risk of impersonation — on April 1.
  • But one high-profile account did lose its blue check over the weekend: the main account for the New York Times, which had previously told CNN it would not pay for verification.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, some VIP Twitter consumers woke up on Saturday expecting to have lost their coveted blue verification check marks in a previously declared purge by Elon Musk. Instead, Twitter appeared to target a single account from a major publication Musk dislikes and changed the language on its site in a way that obscures why users are verified.

In a recent development, twitter had said it would “begin winding down” blue checks granted under its old verification system — which emphasized protecting high-profile users at risk of impersonation — on April 1. In order to stay verified, Musk said, users would have to pay $8 per month to join the platform’s Twitter Blue subscription service, which has allowed accounts to pay for verification since December.

But one high-profile account did lose its blue check over the weekend: the main account for the New York Times, which had previously told CNN it would not pay for verification.

William Shatner is mad he may have to pay to keep his blue Twitter checkmark. Elon Musk says too bad.

After an account that often engages with Musk posted a meme this weekend about the Times declining to pay for verification, Musk responded in a tweet saying, “Oh ok, we’ll take it off then.” Musk then lashed out at the Times — just the latest instance of the billionaire slamming journalists or media outlets — in a series of tweets that claimed the outlet’s coverage is boring and “propaganda.”.

Sources indicate that the weekend moves are just the latest example of Twitter creating confusion and whiplash for users over feature changes — and in this case, not just any users, but many of the most high-profile accounts that have long been a key selling point for the platform. It also highlights how Musk often appears to guide decisions about the platform more by whims than by policy.

It has been revealed that although the Fresh York Times’ main account lost its blue check, its other accounts, such as those for its arts, travel and books content, remained verified. (It’s not clear why the New York Times doesn’t have a gold “organizations” check mark, like accounts for other news outlets, including the Associated Press and the Washington Post.) After its blue check was removed, a spokesperson for the New York Times reiterated to CNN that it does not plan to pay for verification.

Twitter, which laid off most of its public relations staff last fall, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In a separate puzzling move, Twitter’s blue bird logo at the top of the site was replaced on Monday with doge, the meme representing the cryptocurrency dogecoin, which Musk has promoted. The price of dogecoin shot up 20% on Monday.

Musk has been threatening to take away “legacy” blue check marks from people verified under Twitter’s old system since shortly after he bought Twitter last fall.

In early November, Twitter launched the option for people paying for its Twitter Blue subscription service to receive blue checks. The program was swiftly put on pause after being plagued by a wave of celebrity and corporate impersonators, and was relaunched in December.

Twitter also rolled out a color-coded verification system with differently colored marks for companies and government entities, but Musk continued to say that individual users would eventually have to pay for blue checks.

In the days leading up to the blue check purge that wasn’t, prominent customers such as actor William Shatner and anti-bullying activist Monica Lewinksy pushed back against the idea that, as power users that draw attention to the site, they should have to pay for a feature that keeps them safe from impersonation.

Sources indicate that by muddying the reason accounts are verified, the latest label could risk making it easier for people to scam or impersonate high-profile users. Experts in inauthentic behavior have also said it’s not clear that reserving verification for paid users will reduce the number of bots on the site, an issue Musk has raised on and off over the past year.

Musk, for his part, has previously presented changes to Twitter’s verification system as a way of “treating everyone equally.”.

Sources indicate that “There shouldn’t be a different standard for celebrities,” he remarked in a tweet last week. The paid feature could also drive revenue, which could help Musk, who is on the hook for significant debt after buying Twitter for $44 billion.

Musk last week also said that starting on April 15, only verified accounts would be recommended in owners’ “For You” feeds alongside the accounts they follow.

–CNN’s Oliver Darcy contributed to this report.

Newcastle United star Sven Botman has been banned from driving after he was caught using his mobile phone at the wheel.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) confirmed that Botman, 26, pleaded guilty at Newcastle Magistrates Court on Wednesday.

The Dutch international defender was given six penalty points and disqualified from driving for six months, as these were added to points he had already accrued.

The MoJ said Botman was fined £900 and ordered to pay £400 costs and a £360 surcharge.

Court documents show that Botman was in a Land Rover on the A189 Haddricks Mill Road, in Newcastle, on 17 September when he was spotted using his phone.

According to The Sun, the court heard he was filmed by a cyclist while he was stationary in traffic.

The Dutch centre-half was signed by Newcastle in a £32 million deal from French club Lille during the summer of 2022.

Since signing for the Magpies, Botman has made 124 appearances and was part of the squad that won the League Cup in 2025, their first major trophy in decades.

#151207. How cautious investors are struggling to avoid the AI bubble

How cautious investors are struggling to avoid the AI bubble

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1094 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index roared back to life this week after a worrying sell-off recently that saw huge falls in technology and artificial intelligence (AI)-related stocks.
  • After suffering its worst week since the pandemic crash of March 2020, the Nasdaq opened Monday (November 23) nearly 1,700 points, or 7%, higher.
  • The AI trade received a further boost after Nvidia reinstated CEO Jensen Huang on Monday, just 11 days after he was forced to resign amid a scandal involving extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index roared back to life this week after a worrying sell-off recently that saw huge falls in technology and artificial intelligence (AI)-related stocks.

After suffering its worst week since the pandemic crash of March 2020, the Nasdaq opened Monday (November 23) nearly 1,700 points, or 7%, higher.

The AI trade received a further boost after Nvidia reinstated CEO Jensen Huang on Monday, just 11 days after he was forced to resign amid a scandal involving extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

The chipmaker's stock rose more than 30% on the news, opening at nearly $170 (€155.5) per share and recovering most of the losses since last month, when the affair was first reported.

Recent findings suggest that the surge helped propel US stock indices to their best day since last year. But in premarket trading on Tuesday, Nvidia fell about 5%, underscoring the volatility of the market and the risks facing the AI sector and the broader tech industry.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The recent volatility around AI, memory chips and other technology stocks has unnerved even the most experienced and bullish investors.

Yet, those seeking a haven away from the United States stock market, which has enjoyed the majority of the AI hype — along with Taiwan and South Korea — are increasingly finding few places to shelter.

Economists warn that this is partly due to the way index funds, including exchange-traded funds (ETFs), work. These funds hold the pensions and other savings of hundreds of millions of passive investors.

These indices have become increasingly exposed to the AI boom.

Sources indicate that most flagship index funds are keen to ride winners, so they automatically buy stocks according to a organization's market value. The bigger a company grows, the more of it they hold.

The values of Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple, Alphabet and other US technology giants have benefited from this effect, with many soaring after ChatGPT was first released in late 2022.

In a recent development, the US also has an outsized position in funds that track the global economy. Nine of the top 10 holdings of the MSCI All Country World Index (ACWI), an index of more than 2,400 firms across 47 developed and emerging markets, are US Big Tech names.

The other is TSMC, a Taiwanese chipmaker that produces 90% of the high-end AI semiconductors.

Together, these 10 holdings make up nearly a quarter of the index.

Although it's a global index, nearly two-thirds of MSCI ACWI's value is in US-listed companies, even though they make up only around a fifth of its firms.

Industry observers note that "A well-diversified portfolio should ... reasonably represent the entire global economy," Gerd Kommer, founder of the Munich-based asset manager Gerd Kommer Invest, told DW.

It has been revealed that "That's not the case if 70% of the portfolio is concentrated in just one country — the US. The global economy is more resilient than any national economy.".

Kommer, who is known as Germany's "ETF pope," noted investors need exposure to all economic sectors and that no single sector should make up more than a quarter of a portfolio.

Yet, even if investors want to avoid US-dominated World funds altogether, the AI trade still overshadows several other top index funds.

Recent findings suggest that in MSCI's Emerging Market index, for example, the top 10 make up 37.5% of its value and TSMC alone accounts for almost 16%. Tech, chip and internet firms make up eight of the largest holdings, alongside two banks — one Chinese, one Indian.

That matters, according to Dimitri Vayanos, a finance professor at the London School of Economics who studies how passive investing pushes up the prices of the biggest firms.

"My model suggests that the effects of flows into index funds are larger when the large stocks happen to be in the same industry," Vayanos told DW.

When some investors get over-optimistic about a company and push the stock price up, index funds add to that price pressure.

Recent findings suggest that professional investors then often bet against overpriced stocks, a practice known as "shorting," which helps pull prices back down. But that's far riskier with, say, a tech giant than with a small firm.

"Being short 1% of SpaceX involves much more risk than being short 1% of a small firm," noted Vayanos.

Sources indicate that the problem gets worse when the biggest firms are all in the same sector, as they are now. As short-sellers hold back, the biggest stocks climb further, creating what he calls an "amplification-overpricing spiral.".

In a recent development, to cut exposure to AI-related stocks, investors may have to turn to developed market funds outside the US and Southeast Asia. These funds have offered lower returns over the past decade.

In the MSCI Europe, Australasia and Far East (EAFE) index fund, the top 10 holdings make up about 14.5% of the index, about 40% lower than the all-country world index.

EAFE's major holdings include healthcare giant Roche, oil major Shell, HSBC bank and Nestle — the world's largest food and beverage manufacturer.

However, its biggest holding, ASML, is still very much part of the AI trade. The Dutch tech firm sells the equipment that firms such as TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SK Hynix and Micron need to make their chips.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

According to recent reports, if Monday's rebound in the AI trade is sustained, stock prices may move sharply higher over the next few months. Yet if history is a guide, the bubble will eventually burst, leaving both institutional and passive investors nursing heavy losses.

Kommer warned that if the AI bubble bursts, "in all likelihood it will drag down the global stock market," though the damage would be most severe in tech and AI stocks.

Those hit hardest would be retail investors "with heavy portfolio weights in tech and AI stocks," he said, including "a lot of people who have bought individual AI-related stocks on top of their equity ETFs.".

LSE's Vayanos thinks it is still "certainly safer to hold an ETF than to hold individual stocks.".

But as index providers add mega-IPOs such as SpaceX and Claude-maker Anthropic to benchmarks within weeks of their debut, and money continues to pour into passive funds, he warned that "the conditions are present for the effects of our theory to be even stronger.".

#151206. This boiled bag of offal is banned in the US. In Scotland it's a fine-dining treat

📅 03 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1496 w)

This boiled bag of offal is banned in the US. In Scotland it's a fine-dining treat

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1496 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, anthony Bourdain loved haggis.
  • “Don’t let them tell you otherwise, that’s really one of life’s great pleasures,” Bourdain remarked on one of his gastro-curious pilgrimages to Glasgow.
  • A mash-up of diced lung, liver and heart mixed with oatmeal, beef suet, onion and assorted spices, haggis was traditionally made by stuffing these raw ingredients into the stomach of a recently slain sheep and boiling the lot to a state of palatability.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, anthony Bourdain loved haggis. But even the late, great American chef, writer and television host recognized that Scotland’s national dish, with its “sinister sheep parts” wrapped in a shroud of mystery and half-invented history, could be a hard sell.

“Don’t let them tell you otherwise, that’s really one of life’s great pleasures,” Bourdain remarked on one of his gastro-curious pilgrimages to Glasgow. “There is no more unfairly reviled food on Earth than the haggis.”.

A mash-up of diced lung, liver and heart mixed with oatmeal, beef suet, onion and assorted spices, haggis was traditionally made by stuffing these raw ingredients into the stomach of a recently slain sheep and boiling the lot to a state of palatability.

In a recent development, instagrammable is not the word that immediately comes to mind. In our 21st-century world, where “clean” eating and processed pap overlap, haggis can seem like an “Outlander”-style outlier from another age.

Yet, by some alchemy, once cooked to its required “warm-reekin’ (steaming)” state, it adds up to much more than the sum of its modest parts. It’s offaly charm has kept nose-to-tail eating alive among a younger generation of Scots that has largely turned its back on the tripe, liver and kidneys their predecessors enjoyed (or endured).

Carefully prepared, haggis tastes both oaty and meaty; it is dark and crumbly, a little crispy at the edges but still moist; earthy but also savory and spicy; deep-tasting and profoundly warming, the perfect foil for its traditional garnish of floury mashed potatoes and orange bashed turnip.

“It’s like a cuddle for the stomach,” claims Nicola Turner, a 35-year-old office administrator from Helensburgh, a town on western Scotland’s Firth of Clyde.

For children of the 1960s and ’70s, like crime novelist Ian Rankin, haggis meals were a choice between the classic meat-and-two-veg plate and the battered and deep-fried, chip-shop iteration loved by both his friend Bourdain and his quintessentially Scottish detective character, Inspector John Rebus.

Now myriad other treatments have blossomed.

“I’m pretty sure the first time I dined with AB in Edinburgh we had haggis in filo pastry with a jam-style – maybe blackcurrant – sauce,” Rankin recalled. “He was a major fan of haggis and of chip shops. Rebus will have enjoyed the occasional haggis supper from his local chip shop. He was definitely a fan, as am I.”.

“It is all about the spicing and the texture,” claims the Scottish food writer, novelist and cook Sue Lawrence, a champion of haggis’ adaptability for use in other dishes. “If you didn’t know what was in it, you wouldn’t think ‘oh that tastes of liver or whatever.’ It is all nicely chopped up and the oatmeal gives it a lovely texture. It could easily be a nice, significant mince dish.”.

These US restaurants and chefs are James Beard Award finalists.

Lawrence uses haggis as an alternative to beef and pork ragù in lasagna and in her pastilla, a version of the North African dish in which a hand-made haggis from the Isle of Mull substitutes for the traditional poultry or seafood filling. The filo pastry savory is flavored with the spice blend ras el hanout, apricots, chile, orange zest and almonds before being sprinkled with cinnamon and icing sugar.

Such cultural crossovers serve as a reminder that haggis could easily be a dish with nothing specifically Scottish about it at all. Records of similar quick and portable preparations of the fast-perishing innards of sheep and other animals date back to ancient Rome and Greece.

Haggis-like combinations of offal and grains are part of the culinary history of several countries. Spain has chireta, Romania drob and Sweden polsa, while chaudin, or ponce, is a rice and meat-stuffed pig stomach that is a staple of Cajun cooking.

In neighboring England, recipes for “hagese,” “hagws of a schepe,” “haggas” or “haggus” pop up in recipe books published between the 15th and 17th centuries, probably preceding written records north of the border.

Etymological evidence points to the term “haggis” having its roots in Old Norse, suggesting an early version of an oat-and-offal sausage might have arrived in Britain and Ireland on a Viking longboat.

But ever since it was first optioned by the poet Robert Burns in the late 1700s, the haggis backstory has been monopolized by Scotland and the Scots, sometimes mischievously.

It is, according to the kind of lore that Burns engendered, the dish a doughty Highlander would carry with him as he drove cattle through the glens to the markets of the central belt or the perfect picnic for a whisky smuggler plying his illicit trade by moonlight.

Industry observers note that from such romantic notions it was a short step to turning the haggis into a wee wild beastie, one with longer legs on one side that was thus condemned to run round and round whichever hill it lived on. In 2003, a poll of American tourists in Scotland found that one in three of them believed they might encounter such a confused creature on a Caledonian vacation.

Bourdain, a native New Yorker, may have qualified as haggis’ biggest admirer since Burns, but his compatriots at the US Department of Agriculture remain unconverted to offal-filled paunch. Haggis imports into the United States were prohibited in 1971 as part of a ban on the consumption of all livestock lungs. Authentic versions of old school haggis remain culinary contraband in the US, as hard to lay your hands on as Cuban cigars.

In a recent development, across the rest of the world, it’s a different story. According to leading producer Simon Howie, haggis is more widely appreciated and consumed now than it has been since Burns improvised his “Address to a Haggis” for the entertainment of well-to-do Edinburgh acquaintances.

Firmly tongue-in-cheek, the poem lauds the “Great chieftain o’ the pudding race,” as exactly the kind of unpretentious, hearty fare required to nourish a nation of braveheart warriors.

In comparison to the enfeebling foreign muck enjoyed by the capital’s claret-quaffing elites of the time – the olio, fricassée or ragoût that would “sicken a sow” – Burns urges his readers to wonder at the magical impact of haggis on his fellow sons of Scotland’s soil.

As the English translation of the original Scots language version puts it:.

But mark the Rustic, haggis-fed/.

The trembling earth resounds his tread/.

Clap in his ample fist a blade/.

And legs and arms and heads will cut/.

These days synthetic casings have largely replaced stomach but ovine and porcine innards remain at the core of most of the haggis produced in its homeland, stated Howie, who estimates that his company Simon Howie Butchers, accounts for around 60% of the roughly two million haggises produced every year.

Sources indicate that for Howie, versatility, value for money and convenience explain why this staple of the Scottish larder is thriving. Typically haggis retails in Scotland, which accounts for half of global consumption by volume, for around £6, or $7.70 per kilogram ($3.36/pound). That’s around half the price of less expensive cuts of beef or a third of the price of Scotch lamb while enjoying a fairly similar nutritional and calorific profile.

Best Mexican food: 23 dishes to try.

“You can give your kids a meal that is not full of things you don’t want to feed them – for a few pounds you can feed three strapping lads,” Howie mentioned.

“From a kitchen perspective, it is very simple because when it leaves our factory it is already cooked. So when you or a restaurant owner gets it into the kitchen all you have to do is heat it up to be piping hot. It couldn’t be more basic: a student with no cooking skills or a Michelin-starred chef do exactly the same thing to put it out on the plate.”.

Its texture means haggis can also be usefully deployed in fine dining alongside leaner meat like venison or as a stuffing for poultry and game birds. Its spicy intensity means it is also finding uses in canapés and as a crouton-borne garnish for soups.

Buoyant sales are also underpinned by the increasing consumption of haggis in forms inspired by Scotland’s ethnic minorities.

Glasgow’s Sikh community pioneered haggis pakora in the 1990s and samosas, spring rolls and quesadillas have followed in its wake, often using a vegetarian version of the protein in which the offal is replaced by a mix of vegetables, pulses and mushrooms.

Such dishes are more than culinary twists. They are badges of belonging, and an indication that, two centuries after Burns grabbed it for the nation, haggis is as intimately entwined with Scots identity as ever.

Just ask Ross O’Cinneide, a promising 14-year-old fly-half in the junior section of Stirling County rugby club.

“Most of my friends and I like haggis,” he says. “Mum makes it for us sometimes after rugby and it’s got a very nice warming feeling. And it’s nice because it’s purely Scottish.”.

How to become a football referee

📅 01 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1302 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Honestly, for me it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done.
  • Louise Thompson, women's referee pathway officer for the Irish Football Association, international FIFA referee, and PremierLeague referee in Northern Ireland.
  • Looking after female referees within Northern Ireland, trying to recruit, retain and give them experience within their games to pushthrough into top level refereeing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Honestly, for me it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done. You find so much more out about yourself that you probably never knew.

Who are you and what is your job role?

Louise Thompson, women's referee pathway officer for the Irish Football Association, international FIFA referee, and PremierLeague referee in Northern Ireland.

What does a women's referee pathway officer do?

Looking after female referees within Northern Ireland, trying to recruit, retain and give them experience within their games to pushthrough into top level refereeing.

What kind of training do you give to aspiring referees?

So from going through recruitment courses first of all, and then we do the beginners course with referees, just giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge, then we will also do a practical part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we'll go through scenarios, positioning, things around free kick management for example, other set pieces likecorners, penalty setup, what you do as a referee day to day, even pre match stuff as well, so when you arrive at the grounds, how you check the pitch, check all the equipment is there, how you would interact with players, coaches and then just again, maybe createlike a role play sort of environment so that they know that they're not going totally blind into that sort of situation.

Have you always been passionate about football?

Football was a passion of mine, even when I was younger, primary school age, we just didn't have very many female teams, so it normally meant playing with the boys and the boys teams and stuff up until I was about 14, which was the minimum age here you can join senior ladies football team, which is what I did, and played there for 14 years at a club here locally, including up until the Women's Premiership, so it was great to be involved in football, but I always loved watching football, playing football, anything to do with football, I was always there and interested.

How did you go from playing football to being a referee?

Becoming a referee for me sort of happened by chance to be honest. It was during a game, one time I got an injury, quite a bad injury to my knee and then I had seen luckily that the referee course was being advertised. So I signed up for it, but I also signed up for a coaching course pretty much at the same time, maybe about six weeks apart. I wasnât really sure which role I wanted to follow, but over that winter I had been pushed into refereeing a wee bit and said sure, why not, Iâll give it a go, it'd be a bit of extra fitness before my season restarts, and then just fell in love with it from there and never looked back.

What subjects did you study at school and university?

Coming through school I always picked PE, so I did my GCSE PE and then I also did A-level PE and then when I went onto university,I had the sport and exercise science as well within that, so I think it gives you a good understanding of obviously how your body works, and your proposal and training, stuff like that as well so you know when you're working nutrition wise, things that you need to know,especially as you reach the top level, just to make sure that you're getting the most out of your body.

What are your top tips for becoming a referee?

It has been revealed that I would say definitely give it a try for sure. You never know until you do it. I think even when I was a player, I probably never imaginedthat I would be a referee and that I would even achieve and have experienced what Iâve been able to experience. So you never knowuntil you give it a go, but it's also about probably pushing yourself out of your comfort zone, being comfortable with being uncomfortable in situations like that. It's maybe not always as bad as it probably seems it's going to be. There's probably a lot more stigma around being a referee - who wants to be a referee? - but honestly for me, it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done.

With a lifelong love of football, Louise Thompson followed her passion for the game, first as a player and now as a referee. As well as refereeing Fifa and NIFL Premiership matches, she also works for the Irish Football Association as the women's referee pathway officer, recruiting and developing up-and-coming female refs.

Louise Thompson on refereeing the Women's Irish Cup final.

If you're interested in becoming a referee, it's something you can get involved with from a young age through local referee courses. The minimum age to become a qualified referee varies depending on where in the UK you live:.

It has been revealed that in her role as a women's referee pathway officer, Louise oversees latest referees right from the initial recruitment courses stage: "We then do the beginners' course with referees, giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge," she says. "We also do a hands-on part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we go through different scenariosâ¦ exactly what you do as a referee, and day-to-day practical stuff as wellâ¦ The idea is to give them all the basics and fundamentals before they go into a game so that they're prepared.".

It has been revealed that all four UK nations have established pathways for referee development and progression. Starting out at grassroots level, it's possible to progress all the way to Fifa!

According to recent reports, louise's first games were youth games: "I still remember my first game to this day," she says. "It was an under-13 game, and I was definitely the most nervous person on the pitch." She explains: "Over time, you'll get mentors who will come and watch you, give you advice, give you feedback" which will help you to progress to higher levels of the game.

Industry observers note that as well as PE, Louise has found that languages are really helpful in this line of work, "especially when you're dealing with a lot of international games and people coming along," she claims. "If you can learn some languages, it's very, very useful.".

You could get into this role by training with a professional body.

Sources: National Careers Service, GOV.UK, FA, IFA, SFA, and FAW.

Lionel Messi will play his first match in Argentina since his international retirement when he takes part in Carlos Tevez’s testimonial in December.

Messi called time on his 21-year career with La Albiceleste in October, scoring his 126th and final Argentina goal in a 3-0 friendly win over Benin.

It was an emotional send-off for a player that is deified in his homeland, but Argentinians haven’t had to wait long for Messi to come back, with the 39-year-old confirming his next footballing commitment in the country.

The Inter Miami superstar will feature in the testimonial match of his former international team-mate Tevez, which is being held at Boca Juniors’ iconic stadium La Bombonera.

Tevez saw out his career at boyhood club Boca Juniors in 2022, bringing down the curtain on a career that included spells at Manchester City, Manchester United and Juventus.

Tevez made 76 caps and scored 13 times for Argentina, winning an Olympic gold medal with his country at the 2004 Games.

Nicknamed “Apache”, 42-year-old Tevez stated last year he wanted Messi and former United team-mate Cristiano Ronaldo to play on opposing teams in his testimonial.

And while Ronaldo will not be involved barring a dramatic late addition, Messi will turn out for a man he shared the international stage with for a decade.

"It will be a ⁠true honour to welcome the best player in the world to Apache’s last dance," organisers posted on Instagram on Thursday.

Other stars involved in Tevez’s testimonial includes ex-United team-mate Rio Ferdinand, former City strike-partner Sergio Aguero and goalkeeper Gianluigi Buffon, who was Tevez’s captain at Juventus.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It felt like living inside an interactively playable game of Football Manager - or recreating Guy Ritchie’s iconic late-2000s point-of-view Nike advert.
  • According to recent reports, within seconds the novelty wears off and the pressure is on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the basement of a central London WeWork this week, FourFourTwo slipped on a VR headset and stepped onto a virtual pitch.

It felt like living inside an interactively playable game of Football Manager - or recreating Guy Ritchie’s iconic late-2000s point-of-view Nike advert.

According to recent reports, within seconds the novelty wears off and the pressure is on. When a virtual teammate fizzes a pass toward your feet in the middle of a crowded midfield, you rapidly realise just how hard it is to think like a top-level footballer.

Be Your Best (BYB) boast some of the most cutting-edge performance-enhancing technology on the market. Their virtual reality software is designed to train scanning, awareness and in-game intelligence.

Behind it lies nearly three decades of pioneering research by Norwegian sports psychologist Geir Jordet, who began logging how frequently players check their surroundings back in 1997 - armed with nothing more than a notebook and a VCR.

Scanning is the subtle, constant habit of taking mental snapshots of your environment before the ball arrives, and it's what separates good footballers from the greats.

Sources indicate that of the 117 players Jordet studied in his landmark research, the standout was Frank Lampard, who scanned an astonishing 6.2 times every 10 seconds before receiving possession. Lampard Snr. used to bark "Pictures! Pictures!" from the touchline during Frank Jnr.’s West Ham academy days, drilling into the future England international a habit that directly correlates with higher pass completion rates and a greater volume of forward passes.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Industry observers note that timing, though, is everything. Scan at the wrong moment and you miss vital cues on the speed and direction of pressing defenders - FourFourTwo learned that the hard way, frequently dispossessed in traffic or making stray passes.

Inside the headset, BYB drop you directly into real on-field moments recreated from actual matches, complete with four distinct training modes and fresh scenarios released weekly.

It has been revealed that suddenly, you are in the boots of Arsenal captain Martin Odegaard - who famously asked developers to crank the simulation speed up to 120 per cent because standard 100 per cent match pace felt too easy. FFT was playing at 85 per cent. Show-off.

Sources indicate that built-in awareness tests freeze play, turning surrounding players into blank silhouettes, quizzing the user on which team each belongs to. When the ball finally arrives, you have a split second to pick out a pass or pull the trigger.

At the end of each round, the software delivers a brutally honest scorecard, at least that's how it felt to FFT. We were graded on our performance across the following metrics: BYB IQ, scan rate, scan timing, critical scans (checks made in the final moments before receiving the ball), decision-making and overall awareness.

Afterward, a bird’s-eye replay mode allows players and coaches to dissect every scenario from above, effectively handing professionals unlimited 'do-overs' to rehearse how they could have played a situation differently, all without physical fatigue or risking injury.

Recent findings suggest that it is little wonder footballers have taken notice. In the past, Norwegian youth sides featuring Erling Haaland used the technology during their development, while Chelsea midfielder Romeo Lavia is an investor. On the consumer side, everyone from 10-year-old grassroots hopefuls practising in their living rooms to Real Madrid stars Endrick and Aurelien Tchouameni use BYB to sharpen their minds.

Meanwhile, clubs and federations, including Hoffenheim and the Portuguese FA, tap into BYB’s B2B side of things, which includes custom match-scenario builds for academies and Apollo, a separate analytical tool powered by synced 3D tracking and event data. Apollo lets club analysts step inside any player’s first-person POV to review flashpoints and decisions in full 3D.

After 30 minutes in Odegaard’s virtual boots, FFT had improved but we weren't quite at the level of a Xavi Hernandez with a head on a swivel - let's just say our BYB IQ left plenty to be desired.

Be Your Best is offering 30% off annual VR training subscriptions for Black Friday using promo code BF30.

Joe joined FourFourTwo as senior digital writer in July 2025 after five years covering Leeds United in the Championship and Premier League. Joe's 'Mastermind' specialist subject is 2000s-era Newcastle United having had a season ticket at St. James' Park for 10 years before relocating to Leeds and later London. Joe takes a keen interest in youth football, covering PL2, U21 Euros, as well as U20 and U17 World Cups in the past, in addition to hosting the industry-leading football recruitment-focused SCOUTED podcast. He is also one of the lucky few to have 'hit top bins' as a contestant on Soccer AM. It wasn't a shin-roller.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Working on one of the world's biggest football video games is the perfect combination of my two biggest passions, gaming and football.

I'm CJ Ramson. I work on the creation of football video games. I work on Football Manager as an associate QA manager. QA stands for quality assurance.

We're the ones that test the game. We make sure everything works, and we work closely with the developers to try and make the most realistic simulation of football.

In a recent development, growing up, I loved football, whether that was playing football or playing football video games with my friends. I'd always be doing one or the other. With the video games, the thing that really drew me to them was I've always been into the tactical side of the game, either being able to control the players or create your own tactics.

In a recent development, so a typical day for us, we'll get a fresh build in from the developers. We'll test it as a QA team, and we'll look for either bugsor ways that we can improve the game. That can be anything from the runs that players make, to decisions they make on the ball, what the team instructions and tactics do. So there's a lot of areas for us to cover. Our final goal is to make it as realistic to real football as possible.

Sources indicate that so even though my background was in coaching, there was a lot of transferable skills that I learned and developed through my time coaching that I managed to transfer into this. So whether that's being really analytical and having a good eye for detail and knowingwhen to pick things out and what to look for, or it could be things like timekeeping and making sure things run perfectly on time, and working with other people as well. So social skills where you have to work within a team or even lead a team.

The animation he makes, and the ball physics as well, where the ball goes off after the save.".

So as much as I loved playing football, I realised quite early on I probably wasn't going to be a professionalfootballer. But I wanted to work in football and find. So at college, I studied sports science, and that's where I found my love of coaching. I did my FA Level 1 and then went on to do my FA Level 2. After I left college, I got a job at Arsenal, which was unpaid, working with them, learning how to develop my coaching skills. Which then led to me having a full-time paid job at Fulham Football Club, working with the youth teams, working with the academy teams. And then that eventually led to me going to an event. I saw an opportunity where you could apply for a job in Football Manager. It was something that naturally I was interested in, had a conversation with them, and realised it was definitely something that I would love to do.

Recent findings suggest that so I went to the networking event at Kick It Out, and that was an opportunity for me to network with other football coaches, other people within the gaming industries, and have a really good insight to different jobs in football gaming. Without doing that, I wouldn't have the opportunity to meet the people at Football Manager and see a newly introduced job in gaming, which I wouldn't have beenaware of.

One of the highlights of my career so far is working on the in-and-out-of-possession system on FM 26. This is something we see in real football all the time, so being part of the team that brought that to life and brought it into the game was super cool.

Working within the football industry is a dream come true. Being able to work on something that I'm passionate about, that is played and enjoyed by millions of people, is an amazing feeling for me and an amazing opportunity that I have. And yeah, I love it.

Recent findings suggest that ever wondered who makes sure your video games are great? This guy!

CJ works as an associate quality assurance manager on the video game Football Manager. His team test the game to make sure everything works, and collaborate with the developers to create the most realistic simulation of football.

There are lots of different ways to progress in the gaming industry.

Industry observers note that CJ works in the QA (Quality Assurance) team, testing games. In this team, his career progression has followed this path:.

QA tester --> QA lead --> QA manager.

His team is just one of the options, though. "There are lots of other roles within the industry too, including production, game design, social media and development, where developers help to code the game," he explains. "Depending on your skills and interests, there are different pathways you can take that you might enjoy and be suited to.".

There are different roles in video game testing. CJ notes that: "Salaries can vary depending on your role and the company you work for. They can range from around Â£20,000 to Â£50,000 and upwards." The higher salaries in this range could apply when you've gained more experienced and progressed in your career.

CJ is now a quality assurance manager, but he started out as a quality assurance tester. Find out more about the role of QA tester below. This role can have various other job titles, such as games tester, computer games tester, and video games tester.

You could get into this role via a university course, a college course (such as a Level 3 Diploma in Creative Media, an A-level in Computing, or a T-level in Digital Software Development (England only)), an apprenticeship, or applying directly if you have relevant experience.

One person had a worse night than United keeper – the wretched referee

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By the end of another utterly chaotic 90 minutes in the Manchester United soap opera, there was only one person who had endured a worse night than Senne Lammens.
  • Watching this game back will make for grim viewing for the United goalkeeper who, having been one of the club’s shining lights last season, is steadily becoming enveloped in a crisis of his own in this most torrid of campaigns.
  • But Roberto Rosetti, Uefa’s chief refereeing officer, might also want to sit Szymon Marciniak down after this and pick over the Polish official’s own nightmare performance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By the end of another utterly chaotic 90 minutes in the Manchester United soap opera, there was only one person who had endured a worse night than Senne Lammens.

Watching this game back will make for grim viewing for the United goalkeeper who, having been one of the club’s shining lights last season, is steadily becoming enveloped in a crisis of his own in this most torrid of campaigns.

But Roberto Rosetti, Uefa’s chief refereeing officer, might also want to sit Szymon Marciniak down after this and pick over the Polish official’s own nightmare performance. Marciniak denied United two goals, both of which should have stood, and in doing so ended up shining an even more brutal lens on Lammens’s calamitous display.

It has been revealed that united’s Belgian goalkeeper was responsible for both of Sporting’s goals. He needlessly conceded a penalty in the first half, after a rush of blood to the head, that was converted by Luis Suárez, just 75 seconds after he had saved a spot-kick from the Sporting striker.

United had recovered from those bewildering few minutes to lead early in the second half, courtesy of two goals from captain Bruno Fernandes against his old club.

Recent findings suggest that but, 10 minutes from time, Lammens committed the kind of howler that becomes worse and worse with every viewing. In doing so, he handed Sporting an equaliser and ensured United remain without an away win this season.

In a recent development, lammens could have come to meet Iván Fresneda’s cross 100 times and probably dropped the ball only once. It was his and United’s misfortune that it should happen here. Suárez could barely believe his luck, although his finish was still accomplished, an acrobatic overhead kick from close range.

Senne Lammens with a gift for Luis Suárez to equalise for Sporting 🤯 📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/kOQ6HImlVc.

Sources indicate that one of the stars of last season for United, Lammens is being dragged down with the rest of them this time around. He had looked hesitant from the moment he was almost caught dealing with a back-pass by Suárez in the opening minutes. It set the tone for what was to come.

As if Mauricio Pochettino did not already have enough on his plate, United’s newly introduced head coach now has a goalkeeper problem.

Of course, this would not have been as costly a night for Lammens had Marciniak not made such a mess of things himself. United may have been their own worst enemies again, but there was little doubting Sporting were given a helping hand here by some truly wretched refereeing.

The worst of it was the denial of a perfectly legitimate equaliser late in the first half after Youri Tielemans was penalised for a perceived foul – it was nothing of the sort – that the referee had initially not blown for.

And then moments after Suarez made it 2-2, the Sporting goalkeeper Kaique Pereira flapped at Fernandes’s corner and punched the ball into his own net. Kaique’s blunder was already in motion by the time Patrick Dorgu barged into Kaique. But Marciniak was ordered to the pitch-side monitor by Piotr Lasyk, the VAR, and from there, he weakly decided Kaique had been infringed upon by Dorgu. It was a substantial let-off for the goalkeeper and the hosts.

Recent findings suggest that to compounded United’s frustrations, they were then reduced to 10 men late on when Tielemans, who had been booked for protesting over the first disallowed goal, received a second yellow card. It means United have now had four red cards and conceded five penalties in their last five games and, four weeks shy of Christmas, are still searching for a win on the road.

In a recent development, the irony was that, amidst the chaos, there was a lot Pochettino will have liked about the performance. It was far from perfect but United at least had a structure, coherence and confidence about them for long periods. But for Lammens’s shocker and some dubious refereeing, United would surely have claimed just a fourth win this season.

The problem with this United side is they never seem too far away from an act of self-sabotage. Pochettino insisted on the eve of this game that his team were not fragile, but that assessment was challenged in the crazy 160 seconds when United conceded not one but two penalties.

In truth, they could feel hard done to by the award of the first in the 29th minute. Geny Catamo went down far too easily – and very late – after Lisandro Martínez swung out a leg. There was contact but it was of the very minimal variety. Martínez rushed off to Marciniak to remonstrate but his pleas fell on deaf ears. There was a sense of justice, then, when Lammens saved Suárez’s feeble penalty.

You would have thought that would be a confidence booster for Lammens, but in no time he had gone from hero to zero, with worse to follow.

A ball was swept in behind Noussair Mazraoui and Maximiliano Araújo gave chase. There was no need for Lammens to come careering out of goal but that is what he did. When he clumsily blocked off Araújo in the process, Marciniak wasted little time brandishing a yellow card and pointing to the spot. This time Suárez made no mistake from 12 yards.

Industry observers note that what will please Pochettino is United did not crumble again from there. In fact, they rallied and would soon be nursing a sense of injustice for the second time in four days.

Already outraged by the circumstances around Leny Yoro’s rescinded red card against Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday, Pochettino now had to contend with some perverse refereeing from Marciniak.

It has been revealed that tielemans had slipped a pass through to Amad Diallo, with his momentum carrying him into Gonçalo Inácio. Marciniak did not blow his whistle, presumably because in the moment he did not feel a foul had been committed. But after Diallo’s shot was saved and a split second before the Ivorian headed the rebound into the net, the Polish referee blew his whistle.

It's hard to know why this was ruled out 🤯 📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/Pat8nzJiVW.

Tielemans could not believe what he was seeing and, to add insult to injury, was booked for his protestations.

The problem for United was that, because Marciniak had blown moments before Diallo put the ball into the net, VAR were powerless to review the decision.

After the match, Pochettino claimed United were punished by the referee’s decisions.

The Argentine was again in a state disbelief at some refereeing decisions, even though he appeared at pains not to land himself in hot water with Uefa.

“It’s difficult to find a game where you get punished [so much] in one game. We were punished a lot in key actions,” Pochettino mentioned.

On the foul awarded against Tielemans, he added: “I think everyone knows all that was… impossible [to understand]. You know, it’s difficult to understand why that happened on the field.”.

What Pochettino demanded was a strong start after the interval, and he got just that. A third penalty award of the night this time went United’s way. Martínez, who had been operating as an inverted left-back for much of the game, wriggled his way past Eduardo Quaresma before being bundled over from behind by the Sporting defender. Fernandes stepped up and coolly converted the penalty. This time it was Sporting’s turn to implode, even if Fernandes and United’s goal had some good fortune about it.

It has been revealed that fernandes was running to the right when he cut back inside, just outside the penalty area, and struck a speculative left-foot shot at Kaique. There appeared no obvious danger and then the ball seemed to hit a divot in the ground, seemingly created moments earlier by Fernandes as he slid in, and cannoned upwards. The Sporting goalkeeper was thrown by it and the next thing the ball was flying through his hands.

Recent findings suggest that united have had very little in the way of luck this season, so their supporters would argue it was long overdue. Misfortune, in the form of Lammens’s clanger and Marciniak’s refereeing, would soon come back to haunt them, though. What a job Pochettino has walked into.

When it comes to United’s Champions League prospects, the comeback win over Roma at the tail-end of Michael Carrick’s tenure made their position less perilous, but avoiding outright elimination is the first target.

Victor Munoz is in a race against time to be fit for Sunday’s Merseyside derby as Liverpool could be without three midfielders or wingers.

Cody Gakpo will definitely miss the trip to Everton while Ryan Gravenberch is unlikely to be available.

Summer signing Munoz went off in Wednesday’s 3-0 win over Club Brugge with a knee problem he sustained in a collision and while Liverpool are confident there is no major problem, they are waiting to see if he can play at Hill Dickinson Stadium.

According to recent reports, “With Victor, I think the good news is after assessing him, there is no [structural damage] in the knee but he has a substantial knock,” said head coach Andoni Iraola. “He hasn’t trained [on Friday] but he wants to try tomorrow so we will see. I cannot tell you right now.

Gakpo was injured on international duty with the Netherlands and has missed Liverpool’s last two games and Iraola suggested he could be a doubt for next Saturday’s game against Chelsea.

It has been revealed that “Cody is definitely not [in contention for Everton],” Iraola added. “He has a muscle injury so we have to wait a little bit until the process goes on and it heals.

“This kind of injury is normally about two or three weeks. He did it in the last game against Germany so normally so normally it is this timeline. Normally, I don’t like to say timelines with injury because every injury is different and some of them go quicker than others. Normally, this isn’t a big injury but there is something there and you have to give it the time to heal.”.

Midfielder Gravenberch has an matter with his heel and Iraola does not expect him to face Everton.

“I think it is going to be difficult, I cannot say no but this kind of injuries but he has the pain and doesn’t go,” he added.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s Note:  This article was originally published by The Art Newspaper, an editorial partner of CNN Style.

Kwame Brathwaite, the pioneering activist and photographer whose work helped define the aesthetics of the “Black is Beautiful” movement of the 1960s and beyond, died on April 1, aged 85.

His son, Kwame Brathwaite, Jr, announced his father’s death in an Instagram post that read in part, “I am deeply saddened to share that my Baba, the patriarch of our family, our rock and my hero has transitioned.”.

Brathwaite’s work has been the subject of resurgent interest from curators, historians and collectors in recent years, and his first major institutional retrospective, which was organized by the Aperture Foundation, made its debut in 2019 at the Skirball Cultural Center in Los Angeles before touring the country.

It has been revealed that brathwaite was born in 1938 to Barbadian immigrants, in what he referred to as “the People’s Republic of Brooklyn” in Newly introduced York, though his family moved from there to Harlem and then to the South Bronx when Brathwaite was 5 years old. He attended the School of Industrial Art (now the High School of Art and Design) and, according to profiles of Brathwaite in T Magazine and Vice, was drawn to photography by two moments. The first was in August of 1955, when a 17-year-old Brathwaite encountered David Jackson’s haunting photograph of a brutalized Emmett Till in his open casket. The second was in 1956, when — after he and his brother Elombe co-founded the African Jazz Arts Society and Studios (AJASS) — Brathwaite saw a young man taking photos in a dark jazz club without the use of a flash, and his mind became alight with possibility.

In a recent development, using a Hasselblad medium-format camera, Brathwaite attempted to do the same, learning to work with limited light in a manner that enhanced the visual narrative of his imagery. He would soon also develop a darkroom technique that enriched and deepened how Black skin would appear in his photography, honing the practice in a small darkroom in his Harlem apartment. Brathwaite went on to photograph jazz legends performing throughout the 1950s and ’60s, including Miles Davis, John Coltrane, Thelonious Monk and others.

“You want to get the feeling, the mood that you’re experiencing when they’re playing,” Brathwaite told Aperture Magazine in 2017. “That’s the thing. You want to capture that.”.

A 106-year-old from the Philippines is Vogue's oldest ever cover model.

Sources indicate that by the early 1960s, alongside the rest of AJASS, Brathwaite began using his photography and organizing prowess to consciously push back against whitewashed, Eurocentric beauty standards. The group came up with the concept of the Grandassa Models, young Black women whom Brathwaite would photograph, celebrating and accentuating their features. In 1962, AJASS organized “Naturally ’62”, a fashion show held in a Harlem club called the Purple Manor and featuring the models. The show would go on to be held regularly until 1992. In 1966, Brathwaite married his wife Sikolo, a Grandassa Model whom he had met on the street the year prior when he asked if he could take her portrait. The two remained married for the rest of Brathwaite’s life.

By the 1970s, Brathwaite’s focus on jazz shifted to other forms of popular Black music. In 1974, he traveled to Africa with the Jackson Five to document their tour, also photographing the historic “Rumble in the Jungle” boxing match between Muhammad Ali and George Foreman in what’s now the Democratic Republic of Congo that same year. Commissions in this era also saw Brathwaite photographing Nina Simone, Stevie Wonder, Sly and the Family Stone, Bob Marley and other music legends.

Creating for community: The Black designers placing identity and heritage at the center of their brands.

Throughout the ensuing decades, Brathwaite continued to explore and develop his mode of photography, all through the lens of the “Black is Beautiful” ethos. In 2016, Brathwaite joined the roster of Philip Martin Gallery in Los Angeles, and he was continuing to photograph commissions as recently as 2018, when he shot artist and stylist Joanne Petit-Frère for The Fresh Yorker.

It has been revealed that T Magazine’s 2021 profile, published on the occasion of Brathwaite’s retrospective traveling to the Blanton Museum of Art in Austin, Texas, noted that the photographer’s health was failing such that he was unable to be interviewed for the article. A separate exhibition, “Kwame Brathwaite: Things Well Worth Waiting For,” is currently on view at the Art Institute of Chicago, where it will remain until July 24.

Top image: Kwame Brathwaite, “Untitled (Sikolo Brathwaite, Orange Portrait),” 1968.

Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca has downplayed concerns about his team’s togetherness and insisted he is not worried about star striker Erling Haaland following downcast post-match interviews.

City had won 11 of their first 12 matches in all competitions this season but have suffered an alarming downturn in form, only winning two of their last seven games.

Talisman Haaland has also suffered a slump at the same time, scoring just one goal in five games, and cut a morose figure when he was interviewed after a battling 2-2 draw against Napoli in the Champions League on Tuesday.

However, Maresca has insisted their poor run and the Norwegian’s demeanour are not cause for concern.

He noted: “I think Erling is a winner. It's normal that he's not happy when we don't win games but not just Erling, everyone.

“Remember just a few weeks ago he was dancing inside the pitch. You can write and think many different things.

It has been revealed that “Erling is upset. I'm upset because we're not winning games. But this is our job, this is football. That's why I need to maintain the balance.

“He's a nine. They live day by day for goals and winning games. If they don't score or win games they're upset. So I don't think that affects his game but for sure he's not happy not winning games, but everyone is on the same page.”.

Asked whether it has been business as usual in training, he remarked: “He has been good. Yes, normal like since day one. Again, a few weeks ago he was dancing inside the pitch, he was dancing in training. He's happy. It's normal that results affect the mood, that's why we need to win games.

“But I don't see any problem at all with Erling.”.

It has been revealed that the Italian insisted that “transition takes time” and added: “For me, it's completely normal, I'm completely relaxed, no panic at all. I understand that we need to win games because it's our business but for me, it's all normal.”.

Industry observers note that asked whether their string of poor results, which includes a 10-game run without a clean sheet, had affected players’ confidence, he noted: “For sure, when you don't win games, it's not the ideal situation. But we won games at the beginning. We have also seven or eight new players that need to be used to winning games, so it's just a process.”.

City face another significant test as they visit league leaders Arsenal, who are six points ahead, on Sunday.

Recent findings suggest that maresca was insistent that City were not lacking in belief ahead of their trip to the defending champions, saying: “I think we have already shown this season that we are able to win key games, to win away. I don't see any reason why we are not able to win there.”.

Former Liverpool centre-back Dejan Lovren has admitted it will feel 'strange' when Virgil van Dijk eventually leaves Anfield, insisting the Dutchman deserves a fitting farewell whenever the time comes to part ways.

Lovren's role in the team was largely usurped by Van Dijk following the skipper's arrival on Merseyside in January 2018, who has since gone on to help the Reds lift both the Champions League and the Premier League title.

Speaking in an interview via Hajper, the Croatian international suggested that while Van Dijk could still earn a further 12-month contract extension if he maintains his current standards, both the club and player must ensure the timing of his eventual exit is right.

Sources indicate that "It will be strange when Virgil van Dijk leaves Liverpool, but at some point it has to come to an end," Lovren said. "It’ll be crucial for him, the fans and the club that he leaves at the right time. If he stays at his level then you can see a one-year extension, but of course he’ll have to keep proving that on the pitch.

Industry observers note that "But saying that, it’s so important that he gets a good farewell - he deserves it for what he has given to the club for so long, year after year. He has been at the very top.

Recent findings suggest that "He is without doubt one of Liverpool’s greatest ever players. You just need to look at the stats. Look at what he achieved and what he won, it speaks for itself. How many times was he up for the Ballon d'Or or in the FIFPro World 11? It’s not just Liverpool, he's top of the tree.".

Liverpool are already planning for life after their captain, and Lovren also weighed in on whether young defender Jeremy Jacquet has what it takes to fill Van Dijk's boots.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"I hope Jacquet can be the next Van Dijk at Liverpool, but it's really vital to realise why Van Dijk is at the top level, because of his consistency," Lovren added.

Industry observers note that "It's as simple as that. If Jacquet is there for the next seven years, then we can talk about whether he deserves to stay there forever.

Sources indicate that "But if he plays well this year and not well in the next six months, things will change. We know he has the ability, it's about consistency at the end. That's why top players are different from normal players.".

Further up the pitch, Lovren is far more certain of Liverpool's long-term firepower, pointing to the chemistry between Florian Wirtz, Alexander Isak and his former Lyon teammate Bradley Barcola - as well as the eventual return of injured forward Hugo Ekitike.

"When Hugo Ekitike is back? These are beautiful problems, every coach wants that choice," Lovren added.

"Once he comes back alongside Isak, Wirtz, and Bradley, I believe they will have an amazing attack. Quality-wise, find me something better than what Liverpool have to offer.".
